item.title: Jio Platforms Raises About ₹8,110 Cr From Anchor Investors
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Ahead of opening its public issue on Wednesday (October 19), telecom major Jio Platforms has raised ₹8,109.8 Cr from anchor…
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of opening its public issue on Wednesday (October 19), telecom major Jio Platforms has raised ₹8,109.8 Cr from anchor investors. 

The company allotted 7.25 Cr equity shares to anchor investors at a price of ₹1,119 per share, the upper end of its price band. 

Around 2.48 Cr shares, more than a third of the overall, were picked up by 25 domestic mutual funds via a total of 95 schemes. Domestic mutual funds that anchored Jio’s IPO were  SBI Mutual Funds, HDFC Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund, Kotak Mahindra Mutual Fund, among others. 

Besides, 97 Lakh equity shares (13.4% of the anchor round) were picked up by insurance companies and pension funds including Life Insurance Corporation of India, HDFC Life Insurance, SBI Life Insurance, and ICICI Prudential Life Insurance. 

Global investors such as Fidelity, Allianz, BlackRock, Government of Singapore, Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, Goldman Sachs also picked up stakes in Jio ahead of its IPO. 

Earlier in the day, it was reported that the anchor book has attracted demand of more than 30X its size. As per reports, Jio commands a grey market premium of ₹260, indicating a potential premium listing. The company is expected to get listed on the bourses on October 28.

The IPO, which comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, will open for public subscription on October 21 and close on October 23. 

Jio is seeking to raise ₹30,213 Cr at the upper end of the price band, making it India’s largest public offering till date. This pricing would imply a valuation of ₹10.3 Lakh Cr for the telecom major.

The company expects to use the fresh capital generated from the IPO to reduce its subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd’s (RJIL), net debt and interest burden, and improve its leverage.

The proposed repayment covers three external commercial borrowing (ECB) facilities worth a combined ₹29,971 Cr, secured from a consortium of Indian and international lenders, including SBI, Bank of America and First Abu Dhabi Bank. 

The loans were originally raised to fund 5G infrastructure deployment and spectrum acquisition, with repayments scheduled between March and June 2028. Their interest rates range from 1.40% to 5.13% per annum.

The remaining proceeds earmarked for general corporate purposes may be used for strategic initiatives, growth opportunities, capital expenditure, working capital, marketing and other business requirements.

Jio Platforms reported a 9.2% YoY increase in consolidated net profit to ₹7,764 Cr in Q1 FY27, from ₹7,110 Cr a year earlier. Operating revenue rose 11.8% YoY and 2.4% QoQ to ₹39,173 Cr, while gross revenue grew 12% YoY to ₹45,961 Cr.

item.title: FSSAI Crackdown Continues With Fresh Show-Cause Notices Issued To Zepto, Others
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued show-cause notices to quick commerce unicorn Zepto as well…
item.content:encoded:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has issued show-cause notices to quick commerce unicorn Zepto as well as several food and nutraceutical brands amid a broader crackdown on food safety violations. 

The notice against Zepto followed a consumer complaint on social media alleging delivery of expired packets of besan (gram flour). The regulator directed the platform to submit order logs, seller details, warehouse tracking, root-cause analysis, and proof of stock withdrawal and customer refunds. 

Besides Zepto, nutraceutical brands BMS Lifescience and HealthyHey Foods, as well as bakery brand Bakelite Food Processing, received show-cause notices over misleading labelling and advertising. 

  • Bakelite: The parent company behind Pune-based Malpani Foods was targeted over describing its product, ‘Malpani’s Bakelite Puneri Cream Roll’, as ‘creamy’. However, the product includes no cream or  any other dairy-based ingredients but hydrogenated vegetable fat, margarine, and sugar. 
  • BMS Lifescience: The brand was marketing ‘HAOG’s Cranberry Urinary Tract Health Capsules’ under an expired FSSAI registration certificate, and also made health-related claims around disease risk reduction pertaining to the kidney and urinary tract without approval from the regulator. It was also pulled up for misleading usage of the official FSSAI logo, non-compliant use of the claim “as directed by healthcare practitioner”, and making potentially misleading claims online. 
  • HealthyHey Foods: The regulator called out the brand for discrepancies in labelled ingredients across its website and Flipkart regarding its “HealthyHey Nutrition Natural Cranberry Extract 25% Capsules”. It further alleged the brand was making unapproved claims like “100% Natural”; and marketing the product with the FSSAI logo and “FSSAI certified” in a misleading way. 

The regulator has directed all the companies to submit comprehensive written explanations and corrective action reports within stipulated deadlines or face license suspensions and statutory penalties. 

Just days earlier, the regulator pulled up BigBasket and Flipkart over misleading promotions carried by products sold on the respective platforms. 

Besides, the FSSAI has also sanctioned adjudication proceedings against beverage brand Storia. It had earlier flagged the brand’s pomegranate juice for containing only 4% pomegranate juice concentrate and 12% apple juice concentrate, in spite of misleading front-of-pack branding and visual imagery. 

The authority had also cited non-compliant declarations, including prominent “No Added Sugar” claims alongside obscured disclosures, and the unapproved claim “Equivalent to 100% Fruit Juice (Reconstituted)”.

Notably, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) had also fined the brand ₹1 Lakh for misleading consumers. The consumer protection body pulled up Storia for using the branding “100%” in their product labelling, due to reconstituted ingredients and lack of evidence. 

The latest series of notices fits into a larger pattern of the FSSAI identifying illegal food labelling and marketing practices on products sold online. Till now, it has also penalised multiple platforms — Amazon, Bigbasket, Flipkart, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto — for allegedly engaging in misbranding, misleading claims, and sale and display of prohibited or poisonous food articles. 

For Zepto, the fresh regulatory scrutiny adds on to legal issues the quick commerce major has been facing ahead of its proposed public plans. 

Zepto disclosed multiple ongoing regulatory and labour-related proceedings in its updated DRHP, which was filed with the markets regulator SEBI earlier in June.

These include consumer protection cases over alleged dark patterns, food safety violations as well as an Enforcement Directorate inquiry into its ownership structure under FEMA. The company’s subsidiary has also faced allegations of overcharging beyond MRP and misleading advertisements. Other pending matters involve alleged wage underpayment, trade licence violations and food safety issues across several states. 

Besides the regulatory challenges, Zepto had faced unalignment with institutional investors over its IPO valuations which led the company to pause its IPO until May 2027. The quick commerce major is currently chasing a pre-IPO placement of about ₹1,000 Cr.

item.title: Justdial’s Q2 Net Profit Slides 10% YoY To ₹108 Cr Despite 13% Revenue Growth
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Online classifieds platform Justdial’s net profit for the September 2026 quarter (Q2 FY27) dipped 9.7% YoY to ₹107.8 Cr from…
item.content:encoded:
Online classifieds platform Justdial’s net profit for the September 2026 quarter (Q2 FY27) dipped 9.7% YoY to ₹107.8 Cr from ₹119.4 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, the company’s net profit plunged 35.1% from ₹166.2 Cr in the June quarter.

The company’s operating revenue, on the other hand, rose 13.1% YoY and 4.7% QoQ to ₹342.8 Cr.

The decline in net profit came amid a fall in other income, which dropped 25.6% YoY and 58.5% QoQ to ₹54.6 Cr. The company attributed the sequential decline to movements in bond yields. Yields rose around 57 basis points (bps) during the September quarter, compared with a decline of around 44 bps in Q1 FY27, when the company recorded higher mark-to-market (MTM) gains.

The company’s expenses for the quarter rose 15% YoY to ₹262.8 Cr. Tax expenses for the quarter stood at ₹26.8 Cr.

Justdial’s operating EBITDA rose 4.1% to ₹90.7 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹87.1 Cr in the year-ago quarter. However, its operating EBITDA margin contracted 228 bps YoY to 26.4% from 28.7% a year earlier.

The company said investments in AI-led capabilities, automation and B2B expansion accounted for approximately one-third of incremental expenditure during the quarter. These investments are aimed at improving the platform’s capabilities and helping merchants acquire customers and manage their businesses.

Justdial Paid Campaigns, Listings Grows

On the operational front, Justdial recorded 19.84 Cr unique visitors during Q2 FY27, up 0.4% YoY and 2.8% QoQ.

Mobile platforms accounted for 85.1% of the traffic, or 16.89 Cr unique visitors. Desktop and PC platforms contributed 2.45 Cr visitors, accounting for 12.4% of the total, while the voice platform accounted for the remaining 50 Lakh visitors.

While mobile traffic declined 2.1% YoY, desktop and PC traffic grew 24.7%. Voice traffic, meanwhile, fell 9.2% over the same period.

The company’s total active business listings increased 12.2% YoY to 5.74 Cr at the end of September. Justdial added a net 13.1 Lakh listings during the quarter, down 13.8% from 15.2 Lakh additions in the year-ago period.

Paid campaigns on the platform grew 5.2% YoY and 2.7% QoQ to 6.57 Lakh. Total app downloads reached 4.49 Cr, up 7.8% YoY, although average daily downloads declined 21.9% to 6,363.

Alongside its core local business discovery and lead-generation operations, Justdial is expanding its merchant offerings through AI-powered tools and business management products.

The company is developing capabilities to help merchants manage their digital presence, customer interactions and lead pipelines. Its product suite includes JD Business, a dashboard for managing campaigns, enquiries and performance, and JD Omni, which offers business tools, analytics and an online store, alongside a website builder.

Justdial CEO Dinkar Ayilavarapu said the company is now focused on strengthening its core business, helping merchants manage their digital presence and customer conversations, and building products that increase the value of merchant relationships.

The company is also exploring opportunities to expand beyond discovery and lead generation into a broader marketplace of business services and AI-powered tools for merchant operations.

“Looking further ahead, Justdial sees opportunities to extend its platform beyond discovery and lead generation by addressing a broader range of merchant needs. Potential areas include connecting businesses with relevant services through a marketplace, developing AI-powered tools to support business operations, and applying its merchant intelligence and context to enable new digital services,” the company said.

Shares of Justdial ended today’s trading session 2.82% higher at ₹732.55.

Non-institutional investors (NIIs) subscribed to 1.40X of their quota, bidding for 7.18 Cr shares against 5.12 Cr shares reserved for them.

Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) have shown the highest interest in the IPO, oversubscribing their quota by 1.44X. These investors have placed bids for 14.28 Cr shares against 9.89 Cr shares on offer till now.

Following QIBs, non-institutional investors (NIIs) have placed bids for 3.74 Cr shares against 5.13 Cr shares reserved for them, subscribing their quota by 73%. Founded in 2018, Zetwerk operates a full-stack manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories.

It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to manage manufacturing orders across sectors including renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation.

The company has raised over $900 Mn in funding to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and D1 Capital Partners.

On the financial front, operating revenue from continuing operations rose 55.4% to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr in Q1 FY26. Net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the year-ago period.

Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr came from discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included ₹803.2 Cr in exceptional charges from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business.

item.title: Curefoods Pilots Budget Food Delivery App MegaBite
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: In a bid to expand into the budget food delivery segment, cloud kitchen operator Curefoods has begun piloting a new…
item.content:encoded:
In a bid to expand into the budget food delivery segment, cloud kitchen operator Curefoods has begun piloting a new service, MegaBite, in Bengaluru.  

Available on the Play Store and App Store, MegaBite appears to serve dishes — in the range of ₹49-₹199 — from restaurants across its brand portfolio. Dishes from Rolls On Wheels, Olio Pizza, Krispy Kreme, Eatfit, Arambam, among others, are live on the platform. 

The app is currently operational only in Bengaluru’s HSR Layout and claims to charge “no delivery charges” and “no platform fee”. The company’s founder and CEO Ankit Nagori announced the launch on social media today.

MegaBite is being marketed as “built for value-conscious, digitally-savvy consumers” and claims to make food delivery “faster, more affordable, and convenient”.

However, much hasn’t been shared by the IPO-bound company. The company declined to respond to Inc42 on our queries regarding the launch. 

Curefoods follows suit as food delivery competitors are focused on reducing fees and commissions. Rapido’s Ownly, Swiggy’s Toing and Swish Go are some such names that are increasingly doubling down on this proposition. 

To note, this would be the first attempt Curefoods is operating its own delivery platform. It’s unclear as of now if Curefoods itself will handle delivery and fulfilment or if it will join hands with third-party logistics partners. 

Interestingly, rival cloud kitchen operator Rebel Foods has long operated its own delivery app EatSure, which competes with Swiggy and Zomato with offerings from restaurant brands it owns. The startup had also launched a 15-minute food delivery app QuickiES, which it shut down earlier this year, after almost one year of operations. 

Founded in 2020 by ex-Flipkart executive Nagori, Curefoods started off as ‘Eat.fit’, a food brand under the umbrella of fitness startup Cult.fit, but later broke off into a separate business. It has since grown to become a complete house of brands following an elaborate acquisition strategy for expansion. 

The startup has raised $150 Mn to date from the likes of Accel, Iron Pillar and 3State Ventures. Notably, it secured the green light from market regulator SEBI for a public listing around a year ago. The proposed IPO would comprise a fresh issue of ₹800 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 4.85 Cr equity shares. 

However, Curefoods later put its plans on hold after mutual funds reportedly raised concerns around its desired valuation of ₹4,000 Cr, given market volatility.

Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging’s IPO has been oversubscribed 40.82X on the third day of bidding till now. 

Till 13:23 IST, investors have placed bids for 34.80 Cr shares against the 85.26 Lakh shares on offer, as per BSE data.

NIIs are leading demand for the public float till now, placing bids for 18.56 Cr shares against the 18.24 Lakh shares reserved for them. This translates to an oversubscription of 101.78X.

Tonbo started off as a subsidiary of research company Sarnoff Corporation, providing R&D and technology development services. It was bought out in 2012 by promoters and cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza.

Since then, the company has pivoted to design and development of advanced imaging and sensor systems used for surveillance, reconnaissance, targeting, and other military applications. Its product portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, fire-control systems, and missile seekers.

Tonbo handles prototype development, system integration, and qualification testing in-house, while outsourcing manufacturing to partners such as Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology.

On the financial front, Tonbo’s revenue from operations declined 22.7% to ₹362.6 Cr in FY26 from ₹469.1 Cr in FY25. Net profit fell to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr in the previous year. In Q1 FY27, the company reported operating revenue of ₹36 Cr and a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr.

item.title: Hunar Raises ₹40 Cr To Scale Agentic AI For Frontline Hiring
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Hiring thousands of frontline workers (employees who directly provide goods and services to communities) across multiple cities is a coordination-heavy…
item.content:encoded:
Hiring thousands of frontline workers (employees who directly provide goods and services to communities) across multiple cities is a coordination-heavy cumbersome task for HR managers. Recruiters have to call prospective employees, follow up on applications, schedule interviews and keep workers informed through onboarding and training. 

When hiring volumes spike during festive seasons or business expansion, these tasks can quickly become more difficult to solve manually. Bengaluru-based conversational AI startup Hunar.AI is building AI agents to automate these HR workflows. 

The startup today announced the raise of ₹40 Cr ($4.2 Mn) in its Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. Other investors like Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures, PhysicsWallah cofounders Prateek Maheshwari and Alakh Pandey, and MediaMint cofounder Aditya Vuchi also participated in the round. 

Founded in 2022 by Krishna Khandelwal and Shantanu Bhattacharyya, Hunar.AI automates frontline workforce management via its conversational AI agents. These agents help ease various frontline workforce management issues — including hiring, onboarding, training and retention. 

It is targeting businesses that need to recruit and manage large numbers of workers, often across several locations and regional languages.

The startup offers voice AI capabilities in more than 20 languages, including Tamil, Telugu and Kannada. This allows enterprises to communicate with workers in their preferred languages while automating workflows that would otherwise require repeated calls and manual follow-ups.

The startup intends to use the fresh capital to strengthen its AI infrastructure, develop its products and bolster its go-to-market strategy.

“Frontline workforce management is one of the largest yet most underserved opportunities in enterprise AI. Solving it requires more than applying general-purpose models to existing processes. It demands a deep understanding of industry workflows, multilingual capabilities and technology that can reliably execute tasks at scale,” said cofounder and CEO Krishna Khandelwal.

The startup claims its AI agents handled more than 1.5 Cr conversations till September 2026, with volumes doubling quarter-on-quarter. Its customers include Swiggy, Zepto, Aditya Birla Capital, Bajaj Finserv, Croma, Dr Lal PathLabs, 1mg and Starbucks.

AI Targets India’s Growing Frontline Workforce

The startup is targeting a workforce segment that spans quick commerce, ecommerce, logistics, mobility, retail and financial services. These businesses often need to recruit workers quickly across multiple cities, while keeping communication and onboarding processes running at scale.

The market size is also expanding. According to NITI Aayog projections, India’s gig workforce is expected to grow from approximately 1 Cr workers in FY25 to 2.35 Cr by 2029-30.

While more workforce helps in finding the right candidates, keeping applicants engaged, coordinating onboarding and ensuring workers receive the necessary information requires manual effort. This is more relevant when recruitment is spread across regions with different languages.

The startup’s approach is to automate these interactions through conversational agents designed around specific enterprise workflows, rather than offer a general-purpose chatbot. Its ability to handle regional languages and integrate into existing workforce processes will be central to how effectively it can serve large employers.

The latest funding will help the startup build out that technology and expand its reach among enterprises.

item.title: Mobavenue’s Tejas Rathod On The Shift From Ad Optimisation To AI Decisioning
item.dc:creator: Inc42 Staff
item.description: A high click rate cannot tell a fintech company whether a user will complete the KYC. Similarly, downloading an app…
item.content:encoded:
A high click rate cannot tell a fintech company whether a user will complete the KYC. Similarly, downloading an app does not promise a purchase. Yet these remain the metrics that digital advertising has traditionally been built around.

For brands, the real challenge is understanding whether a click or app download will actually translate into a business outcome. As advertisers demand clearer links between media spending and business outcomes, adtech is moving towards systems that can predict intent, learn from downstream behaviour and optimise for what happens beyond the click or install.

This is the shift Mobavenue is targeting. The company processes more than 1.25 Bn data signals a day and has built its technology stack around real-time decisioning and continuous feedback from campaign outcomes. In FY26, it delivered 42.72 Mn outcomes, giving its models a growing base of data to learn from.

At the centre of this is Mobavenue’s Neural Engine, which connects signals, intent and outcomes. Rather than treating a bid, click or install as the endpoint, the system is designed to learn from what happens after that decision and use those outcomes to inform future audience, bidding and budget decisions.

For Tejas Rathod, founder and CTO of Mobavenue, this marks a broader shift in advertising — from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as a decisioning layer across the marketing lifecycle.

In a conversation with Inc42, Rathod explains the technology behind Mobavenue’s platform, how the company approaches privacy and invalid traffic, and why it is building towards an advertising ecosystem that connects awareness, acquisition and activation. 

Here are the edited excerpts…

Inc42: What has been the biggest shift in the Digital advertising industry, and what is driving it?

Tejas Rathod: The biggest shift is the movement from automation towards predictive intelligence and AI autonomy. Earlier, technology helped advertisers execute decisions faster. Today, AI is increasingly being used to anticipate intent, learn from outcomes and make decisions dynamically.

This is being driven by the growing complexity of digital ecosystems, the volume of signals available and the pressure to deliver measurable business outcomes. The next phase is moving from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as an increasingly autonomous decision-making layer.

Inc42: With privacy regulations tightening and invalid traffic remaining a challenge, how has Mobavenue prepared its tech to maintain targeting accuracy and campaign efficiency? 

Tejas Rathod: Privacy has been a foundational consideration in how we have built our tech. Our platforms operate within the requirements of applicable privacy frameworks and regulations across the markets we serve, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework. We also use privacy-conscious approaches to identity, including ID masking and hashing, to derive intelligence without unnecessarily exposing identifiable information.

Our models rely on aggregated, consented signals and behavioural patterns. This lets the system understand user intent and quality while maintaining data safeguards. The objective is to make privacy and targeting intelligence work together, rather than treating them as competing priorities.

Invalid traffic needs to be addressed at multiple points in the advertising lifecycle. Filtering it only after a campaign has run can still result in wasted spend. We therefore use internal invalid traffic detection capabilities at both the pre-bid and post-bid stages.

At the pre-bid stage, the system evaluates available signals and supply characteristics before deciding whether to participate in an auction. This helps reduce exposure to questionable inventory. Post-bid, we analyse delivery and campaign signals to identify patterns that may indicate invalid activity and use these learnings to improve subsequent optimisation.

Fraud detection is also part of our broader machine learning capabilities, alongside audience segmentation, bid optimisation and real-time learning. The objective is to protect both media efficiency and the quality of outcomes.

Inc42: What problem do advertisers still struggle with, and how has Mobavenue built its platform to solve it differently? When did you realise you needed to build more tech in-house?

Tejas Rathod: The fundamental problem advertisers face is not simply acquiring users, but acquiring the right users at the right customer acquisition cost, with a clear path to business value.

We realised early that existing solutions could help us execute media, but they did not give us the level of control and intelligence required to consistently optimise towards the right customer acquisition cost (CAC). That led us to build our tech stack in-house, layer by layer.

Our AI systems analyse billions of signals to identify users with a higher likelihood of conversion, while enabling budgets to be dynamically allocated based on those signals. The objective is not to optimise for media metrics in isolation, but to continuously improve the efficiency and quality of user acquisition. That shift, from media execution to technology-driven outcome optimisation, has been central to how we have built Mobavenue.

Inc42: As brands shift from clicks and installs to outcome-based ROI, how does your engineering team build predictability into the platform? What tech decisions have helped Mobavenue operate at the scale of 1.25 Bn data signals a day?

Tejas Rathod: Predictability starts with the quality and depth of the signals available to the system. Our engineering stack looks at large volumes of consented data signals and combines them with audience segments, behavioural patterns and relevant user attributes to understand intent. 

The objective is not simply to identify a user who may click or install, but to predict the probability of completing the business outcome that the advertiser values.

For example, in a fintech journey, that could extend beyond an app install to KYC completion, investment or loan conversion. Our Neural Network continuously feeds outcomes back into the system, allowing models to learn which signals correlate with quality conversions and improve subsequent decisions.

Adtech is a fast-moving environment where the value of a decision can change within milliseconds, while expectations around accuracy and outcomes continue to increase. So, from the beginning, we made a few deliberate technology choices: real-time decisioning, proprietary intelligence and a common data layer rather than multiple disconnected systems.

The other important decision was to build a closed feedback loop into the platform. Every campaign outcome generates a new learning signal that feeds back into our models, helping improve subsequent decisions around audiences, bidding and budget allocation. 

In FY26, we delivered 42.72 Mn outcomes, and this scale of execution gives our models a continually expanding base of learning. For us, maintaining performance at scale means combining speed with continuous learning, so that every decision becomes more informed by the outcomes that came before it.

Inc42: Mobavenue recently formalised its focus on AI infrastructure. How does its Neural Engine think differently from traditional programmatic advertising, and what led you to build an intelligence layer across the marketing lifecycle?

Tejas Rathod: Traditional programmatic advertising is largely designed to make the best decision for the immediate media event, such as whether to bid, how much to bid, or which audience to target. Our Neural Engine is designed to learn from what happens after that decision. We have moved our core decisioning from rule-based and traditional ML systems to a unified neural network architecture built around three stages: process signals, predict intent and produce outcomes.

It continuously processes signals, predicts intent and evaluates downstream outcomes, creating a closed feedback loop where every outcome becomes a new signal for the next decision. So, intelligence does not simply optimise a campaign; it continuously learns what drives quality outcomes and adapts its decisions accordingly.

The adtech ecosystem has become good at automating individual parts of advertising, but intelligence is still fragmented across the marketing lifecycle. Planning, audience selection, campaign execution, creative and reporting often sit across different systems, which means marketers still have to connect the dots and move decisions from one stage to another.

We saw that the next opportunity was not simply to automate another task, but to create an intelligence layer that could continuously connect signals, decisions and outcomes. That thinking led to the Mobavenue Neural Engine. It brings together our proprietary advertising intelligence, first-party platform intelligence and real-time business context to make recommendations that become more relevant as the system learns.

The larger shift is from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as a decisioning layer across awareness, acquisition and activation. Our Neural Engine is designed to connect planning, execution, optimisation and reporting, while keeping the marketer in control. For us, the future is not just about making advertising faster. It is about making the entire marketing lifecycle more intelligent, connected and outcome-driven.

Inc42: The company closed FY26 with ₹218 Cr+ in revenue and roughly a 20.8% EBITDA margin. How closely do you tie your product roadmap to these metrics, and which products drove the growth?

Tejas Rathod: For us, the product roadmap is primarily driven by the opportunity we see in the market. Financial performance is an important validation, but we do not build products simply around a revenue or EBITDA target. We look at where consumer behaviour, technology and advertiser demand are moving, and then build around those opportunities.

FY26 is a good example of this approach. Our existing platforms, particularly PrsmX and the Neural Engine across all products, were significant contributors to our revenue momentum during the year. These products continued to evolve as we saw greater demand for AI-driven optimisation and outcome-based advertising.

PiiX is the next example of that product philosophy. We identified a significant opportunity in the Apple Search Ads ecosystem and launched PiiX in Q1 FY27 as a dedicated intelligence platform for that high-intent environment. So, the roadmap is driven by market opportunity, while revenue and profitability validate whether we are creating meaningful value from those investments.

Inc42: Over 73% of your revenue now comes directly from brands. What did you change about the platform and reporting to make enterprise clients comfortable managing campaigns directly?

Tejas Rathod: Direct advertiser relationships required us to rethink the platform experience end to end. We undertook a significant overhaul of the interface, underlying infrastructure and reporting capabilities to make the system more robust, intuitive and user-friendly for enterprise teams.

We also expanded the platform’s functionality across campaign planning, execution, creative intelligence and measurement. A key focus was making reporting easier to understand while providing the level of granularity that enterprise advertisers need to evaluate performance, understand where their budgets are being deployed and make informed decisions. 

The objective was to create greater transparency without adding unnecessary complexity. And the larger goal is to make sophisticated technology accessible without requiring the user to deal with the complexity underneath it.

Inc42: How has Mobavenue grown over the past year? Can you share any numbers around campaign performance, advertiser ROI or CAC that highlight the platform’s impact?

Tejas Rathod: Over the past year, our growth has been closely tied to how effectively our technology can improve measurable outcomes for clients. We operate on an outcome-as-a-service model, which means we grow when our clients grow. Revenue per outcome (RPO) is an important business metric for us because it reflects the value generated from every measurable outcome.

Our RPO increased from ₹44.99 in Q1 FY26 to ₹48.44 in Q4 FY26, while quarterly outcomes grew from 9 Mn to 12.61 Mn.

At the campaign level, this translates into measurable performance. Snabbit achieved 5X growth in installs and 10X growth in first-time purchases through precision programmatic optimisation. 

For boAt, our PrsmX platform delivered a 91% view-through rate (VTR), along with a 14% increase in aided awareness, a 20% increase in brand favourability and a 19% increase in purchase intent.

Inc42: Where do you see the next big opportunities for adtech?

Tejas Rathod: I see opportunities across three fundamental areas of brand growth: awareness, acquisition and activation. These are not isolated businesses anymore. A brand may need to create awareness, acquire a user and then activate or retain that user, with intelligence from each stage informing the next. 

That is the direction in which we are building Mobavenue. Our products address these stages, but they are increasingly connected through a common intelligence layer that allows data and learnings to move across the consumer journey.

Inc42: Five years from now, what do you want Mobavenue to be known for?

Tejas Rathod: Five years from now, I would like Mobavenue to be recognised as a technology company that covers the broader digital growth ecosystem, not just advertising. We see significant opportunities across adtech, martech and monetisation technology, and our ambition is to build proprietary platforms across these areas that work together intelligently.

item.title: MeitY Asks Meta To Review Content Recommendation Algorithms
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: The Centre has asked Meta, which operates Instagram and Facebook, to review its recommendation algorithms to prevent disproportionate exposure to…
item.content:encoded:
The Centre has asked Meta, which operates Instagram and Facebook, to review its recommendation algorithms to prevent disproportionate exposure to a limited set of narratives and strengthen checks on content that could cause public disorder or incite violence. 

In an advisory dated October 10, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) directed Meta to provide adequate context for photographs, videos, graphics and other content depicting ongoing public events, particularly when their authenticity, date, location or circumstances may not be readily apparent to users, according to PTI.

The advisory also called for a review of Meta’s recommendation and content-ranking mechanisms to prevent potentially misleading, manipulated or out-of-context material from being disproportionately amplified or repeatedly recommended to users.

“Ensure that recommendation systems do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives, and endeavour to provide appropriate diversity of relevant and credible information,” the advisory said.

It also called for stronger mechanisms to rapidly identify, review and escalate content that gains significant reach through recommendation systems and could potentially cause widespread public confusion, apprehension, violence, or disturbances to public order.

The advisory came amid protests in Delhi by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Similar concerns over content moderation were raised by the government earlier, following a CJP protest at Jantar Mantar in June.

While the advisory does not specify what prompted the government’s move, IT Ministry sources told PTI that agencies had flagged concerns over Meta’s recommendation algorithms, which allegedly appeared to favour certain types of content over others.

What MeitY Wants Meta To Change

The advisory asked Meta to provide users with a diversity of relevant and credible information through its recommendation systems.

It flagged videos, images, statements and graphics relating to public events that were being “prominently displayed and recommended to users” across Meta’s platforms. It warned that such material, when circulated without adequate context or amplified disproportionately, “may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity”.

MeitY asked the company to pay particular attention to old or selectively edited visuals presented as current events, unverified claims about emergencies and police action, and audio-visual material relating to law-and-order situations that lack adequate context. It also called for stronger mechanisms to identify and review content that could incite violence or other unlawful activity.

The advisory invoked the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the IT Rules, 2021, which require intermediaries to exercise due diligence and inform users about prohibited content. It also called for timely cooperation with law enforcement agencies and other authorised government bodies.

Meta was asked to implement the measures “with immediate effect” and inform the ministry of the action taken. The advisory stated that any action must comply with applicable laws while respecting lawful expression and legitimate public discourse.

The directions have drawn criticism from digital rights advocates over its potential implications for freedom of expression and content moderation.

Apar Gupta, founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation, described it as a “continuing censorship directive”, arguing that it was not legally binding. Gupta urged MeitY to withdraw the advisory and called on Meta to publicly disclose every takedown and instance of downranking carried out in response to it.

He also questioned the legal basis for the directive, arguing that phrases such as content circulated “without adequate context” and periods of “heightened public-order sensitivity” were not tied to specific provisions of the IT Act or the IT Rules.

item.title: Even Healthcare Raises $50 Mn To Expand Hospital Network Across Bengaluru
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Bengaluru-based managed care startup Even Healthcare has raised $50 Mn (about ₹475 Cr) in a Series B funding round led…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based managed care startup Even Healthcare has raised $50 Mn (about ₹475 Cr) in a Series B funding round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures, with participation from Alpha Wave.

The all-equity primary round takes its total funding to over $120 Mn, the startup said in a statement.

Even will use the proceeds primarily to expand its hospital network in Bengaluru. It plans to open another hospital by the end of 2026, followed by three more by the end of FY27. It currently operates two multispeciality hospitals on Race Course Road and in HBR Layout.

The startup plans to enter other cities after strengthening its Bengaluru presence. “We want to make sure that Bengaluru patients and members are pretty well served,” cofounder Mayank Banerjee told Inc42.

Even said its valuation had tripled since its previous fundraise 18 months ago, without disclosing its latest valuation. The startup last raised $20 Mn earlier this year to expand its hospital network and launch new facilities.

Founded in 2020 by Banerjee, Matilde Giglio, and Alessandro Ialongo, Even offers an integrated managed care model combining preventive care, outpatient consultations, diagnostics, insurance access, hospitalisation, and post-discharge recovery.

The startup aims to reduce healthcare costs by managing patients’ health beyond individual hospital visits. Its services include telemedicine, at-home blood tests, and medical guidance, alongside cashless hospitalisation through insurance partners.

Even employs salaried doctors whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed or revenue generated. The startup said it assesses doctors on patient outcomes, recovery timelines, and re-admissions.

Banerjee said around 85-90% of Even members living near one of its Bengaluru hospitals choose the startup for their healthcare needs.

Even also uses an AI-based quality system to review cases against clinical protocols in real time. It recently launched Even Spotlight, a dashboard tracking clinical outcomes and patient-reported metrics.

The startup said unplanned re-admissions in programmes run with insurance partners remained below 1%, compared with an industry range of 8-15%. It also claimed average hospital stays were 40% shorter, while proactive care helped more than 200 members avoid hospitalisation, saving an estimated ₹15 Cr to ₹16 Cr.

Even claims to serve more than 2.5 Lakh members across 10 cities, having tripled its membership over the past year.

The hospital expansion follows reports in August that Even laid off around 350 employees as it scaled down its insurance business and shifted resources towards a hospital-led healthcare model. The cuts affected 30-35% of its workforce across multiple teams.

Update| October 19, 17:48

Shares of Urban Company ended today’s trading session 9.92% lower at ₹142.6 apiece on the BSE.

Original| October 19, 12:28 IST

Shares of home services company Urban Company slumped 9.5% to ₹143.30 apiece on the BSE during early trading today, following its Q2 FY27 results and board approval for a fundraise of up to ₹2,500 Cr.

At 12:10 IST, the stock was trading 8.56% lower at ₹144.75 on the BSE. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹22,323 Cr (about $2.7 Bn) at the time.

Urban Company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹182.5 Cr for Q2 FY27 on Friday (October 16) as against a loss of ₹59.3 Cr a year earlier and ₹92.1 Cr in the preceding quarter. 

Operating revenue rose 41% to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, total expenses increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr, driven largely by higher spending on its quick household help business, InstaHelp.

The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr, including what it described as a “deliberate” ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding the vertical, adjusted EBITDA stood at ₹30 Cr. 

The company’s board also approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr through equity shares and/or convertible securities via preferential allotment or private placement.

Urban Company said the proceeds would strengthen InstaHelp’s market leadership, support investment across its three businesses, and fund potential acquisitions.

It is also exploring entry into the residential air conditioner market under its consumer appliances brand ‘Native’, which currently sells water purifiers and smart locks. Management said it could meet its profitability targets without additional capital, although InstaHelp’s losses limited its financial flexibility.

Despite the rise in its loss, Emkay Global Financial Services maintained its ‘Buy’ rating for Urban Company and raised its target price to ₹200 from ₹190, citing growth opportunities across its segments and the strength of its core business.

The brokerage highlighted low penetration of its core services, expansion into Tier II cities, improving international profitability, and the Saudi Arabia business’ progress towards breakeven. It also identified Native as a growth opportunity and said InstaHelp was driving higher customer engagement.

item.title: Zerodha Launches US Stock Investing, Offers Access To 2,000 Stocks
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Discount brokerage Zerodha has launched US stock investing in beta mode on its Kite platform, allowing Indian investors to buy…
item.content:encoded:
Discount brokerage Zerodha has launched US stock investing in beta mode on its Kite platform, allowing Indian investors to buy shares of US-listed companies and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) through their existing accounts.

The offering provides access to up to 2,000 US-listed companies and around 1,000 ETFs. It also supports fractional investing, allowing users to invest in a portion of a share with investments starting at $1.

Resident Indian individuals can activate the international investing segment through Kite without opening a separate demat account and transfer funds from their linked Indian bank accounts to a dollar-denominated wallet.

Users can fund their dollar-denominated wallets through netbanking from linked accounts at supported Indian banks. UPI, debit cards, and credit cards are not supported.

Zerodha is charging brokerage of 0.1% of the trade value, subject to a minimum of $0.01 and a maximum of $10 per executed order. An 18% GST applies to brokerage.

Other charges include an IFSCA turnover fee of 0.005% on trade value, along with applicable US regulatory transaction fees on sell orders.

For currency conversion, Zerodha’s guide lists a negotiated bank markup of 0.5%-1.2% over the RBI reference exchange rate.

The service supports delivery-based investing, fractional ownership and SIPs in eligible US stocks. Intraday and margin trading are not available for international equities, and users cannot apply for US IPOs through the platform.

The service is routed through BSE’s India INX Global Access at GIFT City. The underlying US securities are held through a US brokerage partner rather than in an Indian demat account.

Brokers Expand Into US Equities

Zerodha’s launch comes after the startup, along with peers like Groww, Upstoxx and Angel One, received approval from the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) in June to offer investors the option to buy international and US stocks from GIFT City. 

Following this, Groww introduced US stock investing to its customers in September, partnering with US brokerage infrastructure provider Alpaca Securities. Its platform provides access to more than 10,000 US stocks and ETFs and supports fractional investing.

Meanwhile, Upstox launched US stock investing in September, offering access to more than 8,000 US-listed stocks and over 2,000 ETFs, with fractional investments starting at $1.

Earlier today, Angel One also begun rolling out US stock investing on its app to select users, with a wider rollout planned by mid-November. It is offering fractional investing, and will charge zero brokerage till December 2026, post which it will be priced at 0.1% per trade, subject to a minimum of $0.99.

Stockbrokers are diversifying their offerings beyond domestic equities amid a rising demand from Indian retail investors seeking direct exposure to international markets. 

This is driven by a desire to hedge domestic concentration, access global technology megatrends like AI, cloud computing, and semiconductors, and diversify geographical risk, opening up their portfolio to top global companies like NVIDIA, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon. 

The prospect of high-profile US listings, particularly in the technology sector, including companies such as SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, have also drawn investor attention. 

Zerodha and Groww have joined existing providers such as INDmoney and HDFC Securities in providing US investing.

item.content:encoded:
Inside UC’s ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise Plan

A year after listing, Urban Company is back in the market for more funds. The company plans to raise ₹2,500 Cr as it chases profitability, eyes new businesses and fights a costly battle for home services supremacy. Will the fresh capital fortify UC’s competitive posture?

A Bigger War Chest: Urban Company’s board has approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr through equity or convertible securities. While it is yet to decide on the route for the fundraise, the management believes that the proceeds would absorb short-term operational burn without constraining internal cash flows.

The ₹2,500 Cr Buffer: While the company maintains that it can reach EBITDA breakeven by FY28 without fresh capital, the fundraise provides balance sheet flexibility. Simultaneously, the capital buffer will also enable UC to fund new products, execute new acquisitions and expand internationally without compromising its core margins.

The InstaHelp Drag: The timing is significant. The company’s net loss more than tripled YoY to ₹182.5 Cr in Q2 FY27. Largely to blame for this was the loss from its quick service vertical, InstaHelp, and continued investments in the business. What has not helped is the intensifying competition from Snabbit and Pronto, which is forcing UC to spend heavily on user acquisition, retaining gig workers and market expansion.

The Native Expansion: Parallely, UC is also foraying into the residential AC market under its Native brand. The new venture will rely solely on the UC app for distribution, focusing its initial years on product feedback and calibrated capital allocation. While service demand does not automatically translate into appliance sales, the company will be banking on its years of data on consumer pain points and product gaps to carve its niche. 

With InstaHelp consuming cash and Native entering a new category, can Urban Company use the potential ₹2,500 Cr war chest to enter and dominate Indian homes? Let’s find out…

From The Editor’s Desk

Burma Burma All Set For IPO

  • The restaurant chain’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Pvt Ltd, has filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale component of up to 2.8 Cr shares.
  • Founded in 2013, Hunger Pangs operates Burma Burma, which serves vegetarian Burmese cuisine. It operates 22 restaurants across nine cities. The startup also plans to open Japanese restaurants and noodle shops under a new brand. 
  • On the financial front, the company saw its operating revenue zoom 46.6% YoY to ₹155.5 Cr in FY26, while net loss widened nearly 31X YoY to ₹15.4 Cr. Hunger Pangs also reported a top line of ₹53.7 Cr against a profit of ₹1.1 Cr in Q1 FY27.

ixigo’s Q2 Snapshot

  • The travel tech major reported a net profit of ₹63.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 against a loss of ₹3.5 Cr in the year ago quarter. The OTA swung to the black on the back of a one-time gain, improving margins and operating revenue rising nearly 13% YoY to ₹321 Cr.
  • Train remained ixigo’s largest revenue-generating segment, with GTV rising to ₹2,256 Cr during the quarter. The flight GTV also rose 37% YoY to ₹2,184.3 Cr, while bus booking generated a GTV of ₹752.7 Cr. 
  • Going forward, the listed OTA plans to continue investing in hotels and AI as “key drivers” of its long-term growth. At the end of September 2026, ixigo’s hotel inventory covered more than 70,000 properties across 1,100 towns.

Startup Funding Rebounds

  • Indian new-age tech ventures cumulatively bagged $236.2 Mn last week, up 92% from $123 Mn in the preceding week. Deal count, however, stayed at 25. Boldfit and GreenCell Mobility took the biggest cheques home at $42 Mn and $35 Mn, respectively.
  • AI startups dominated the funding charts last week and lapped up $53.4 Mn across six deals. Following suit was ecommerce, which emerged as the second-most funded sector and secured $48.3 Mn.
  • Early-stage funding activity remained strong as pre-seed and seed-stage startups raised $25.9 Mn across 11 deals last week. Meanwhile, Accel emerged as the most active investor last week and backed four startups. 

Mixed Week For Startup Stocks

  • Of the 67 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage, 31 gained between 0.03% and 17.63% last week. The remaining 36 declined by as much as 18.43%. AceVector and Tracxn emerged as the biggest losers, while Yudiz and Nazara gained the most.
  • The combined market capitalisation of the 67 new-age tech companies rose 3.8% to $160.6 at the end of last week, up from $154.71 Bn in the preceding week.
  • Investors will track September infrastructure output, PMI readings and RBI monetary policy committee meeting for market cues this week. Inflationary pressures, crude oil prices and foreign investor flows will also decide market direction.

Ekart Mixed FY26 Show

  • Instakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in FY26. The company managed to narrow its losses by 98.3% YoY to ₹26 Cr in the fiscal under review compared to ₹1,508 Cr in FY25.
  • The losses declined despite Ekart’s top line falling 4.2% YoY to ₹13,194 Cr in FY26. Of this, Flipkart itself contributed ₹9,112 Cr, or about 69% of the total operating revenue. Meanwhile, expenses stood at ₹13,638 Cr in FY26, albeit down 13% YoY. 
  • Founded in 2009, Ekart offers fulfillment services not only for Flipkart and Myntra but also for external D2C brands, online sellers and retailers. The logistics platform claims to operate 70 fulfilment centres, 80 sortation facilities and 3500 delivery hubs across India.

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

How EdgeVerse Is Helping Two-Wheelers Spot Danger

India is home to one of the largest two-wheeler markets in the world. Yet, collision-prevention systems remain largely limited to cars. Enter EdgeVerse, a startup building an AI-powered stack to bring advanced rider assistance features to two-wheelers.

ADAS For Bikes: Founded in 2023, EdgeVerse is developing Perceiva, an advanced rider assistance system (ARAS), for two-wheelers. Akin to ADAS for cars, the system combines camera, radar and GPS inputs to deliver real-time perception and safety for two-wheelers.

EdgeVerse’s Tech Stack: The startup’s hardware platform is designed to run perception workloads at the edge, reducing dependence on cloud connectivity. The startup also claims that its technology can work with existing camera and radar architectures, enabling OEMs to add safety intelligence without significantly increasing vehicle cost or hardware complexity.

The Road Ahead: Having already conducted road testing, EdgeVerse now plans to enter the market through OEM partnerships in late-2026. It has also set its eyes on experimenting with use cases like industrial automation and other edge-AI applications. Going forward, the startup plans to accelerate the development and commercialisation of its perception technology. 

With the Indian ADAS market projected to become a $3.1 Bn opportunity by 2031, can EdgeVerse make rider safety a standard feature on India’s two-wheelers?

item.content:encoded:
Menswear brand The Pant Project has raised ₹109 Cr (about $11.5 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India) to expand its offline presence and broaden its apparel portfolio.

Existing investor Sorin Investments also participated in the round, alongside family offices and angel investors, including Anisha Saraf, B&K Securities, MGA Ventures, and B2V Ventures.

The latest round takes the startup’s total funding to over $15.75 Mn. It previously raised $4.25 Mn in a Series A round led by Sorin Investments in 2024, following four years of bootstrapping.

Separately, The Pant Project secured venture debt financing from Alteria Capital for an undisclosed amount.

The startup plans to increase its exclusive brand store network from 25 to 150 over the next two to three years. It will also deploy the fresh capital to broaden its menswear portfolio, with a focus on jeans, athleisure, and casualwear.

While it already sells jeans and products such as sweatpants, joggers, and shorts, the startup said it intends to build a broader menswear business beyond its core bottomwear offering.

Founded in 2020 by brothers Dhruv Toshniwal and Udit Toshniwal, The Pant Project started as a digital-first brand specialising in bottomwear for Indian men. Its portfolio includes products such as Malai Pants and Inklock No Fade Black Jeans.

The startup offers more than 300 stock-keeping units (SKUs), spanning custom-made bottomwear and ready-to-wear apparel for men and women. It sells through its website and online marketplaces, including Myntra and Amazon.

“The Pant Project started as a digital-first brand. That foundation gave us the data, the product knowledge and the brand equity to now go deep offline,” said founder and CEO Dhruv.

According to Mandar Dandekar, partner at Sorin Investments, the startup’s revenue has grown more than fivefold since its Series A round, supported by repeat purchases.

The Pant Project operates in a competitive menswear market, alongside digital-first brands such as Snitch, Bombay Shirt Company, Rare Rabbit, and established players like Blackberrys, Raymond, and Louis Philippe.

The fundraise comes amid continued investment in offline expansion by D2C fashion brands. Last week, menswear brand KISAH raised ₹35.9 Cr in a Series A round led by Fireside Ventures, primarily to expand its retail network.

At the heart of this funding push is the growing Indian menswear market, which is seeing brands compete across price points — from affordable fashion to premium apparel. The market is projected to reach $42.44 Bn by 2034 from $23.5 Bn in 2026, clocking a CAGR of 7.24%, according to IMARC Group.

item.title: Will The Jio Platforms IPO Live Up To Its Billing?
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: It’s already called the biggest IPO in India, but Reliance Industries Limited is leaving no stone unturned. RIL chairman Mukesh…
item.content:encoded:
It’s already called the biggest IPO in India, but Reliance Industries Limited is leaving no stone unturned. RIL chairman Mukesh Ambani has reportedly urged all 4.2 Lakh Reliance employees to invest in the IPO, even paying their salaries in advance. 

Whether this is a show of strength or a safety net will only become clear after October 23 when the Jio Platforms IPO closes. RIL employees or not, investors will need to look at what can drive Jio’s growth from here and whether its digital businesses can deliver meaningful returns for those who back its IPO .

The company’s ₹30,213 Cr IPO will open for subscription on October 21 and close on October 23, with a price band of ₹1,065–₹1,119 per share. At the upper end, the issue values Jio Platforms at around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr. The offering comprises a fresh issue of up to 27 Cr equity shares, with the proceeds earmarked primarily for repaying certain borrowings of its material subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm (RJIL). 

The breadth of the company is central to the investment case. Jio has spent years building a nationwide digital infrastructure and a large base of users who consume data, content and connected services. 

Jio Platforms reported revenue from operations of nearly ₹1.47 Lakh Cr in FY26, up from ₹1.28 Lakh Cr in FY25, while net profit rose to ₹30,049 Cr from ₹26,109 Cr. RJIL had 533.3 Mn customers as of June 30, 2026, and Jio’s network carried around 60% of India’s wireless data traffic in FY26, according to its RHP. Its proposition, however, extends beyond mobile connectivity to fixed broadband, entertainment, cloud services, enterprise solutions and artificial intelligence (AI).  

But with most of the proceeds earmarked for debt repayment, it is imperative to examine how Jio Platforms makes money, whether its digital and AI ambitions can become meaningful growth engines, and what investors need to weigh against its scale and profitability.

How Jio Platforms Makes Money

Jio Platforms’ multifaceted business model rests on a simple premise: attract customers through connectivity and earn more from them through a range of digital services.

The company operates through RJIL, its licensed telecom subsidiary, which provides mobile connectivity and fixed broadband. Other offerings span digital entertainment, gaming, cloud storage, smart-home solutions, enterprise connectivity and managed services. These include JioFiber, JioAirFiber, JioTV+, JioSaavn, JioAICloud, JioPC and JioBrain.

For now, the financial trajectory remains closely linked to the underlying telecom business.

Jio Platforms’ EBITDA rose 18.8% to ₹76,255 Cr in FY26, while the EBITDA margin expanded to 51.91% from 50.05% in FY25. “The margin improvement suggests that the company has been able to grow earnings faster than revenue, although investors will need to track how future network investments, depreciation and financing costs affect profitability,” an analyst at a leading brokerage firm said.

The next question is how much more Jio can earn from its existing customer base.

In the quarter ended June 2026, Jio’s average revenue per user (ARPU) rose 3.26% to ₹215.60 compared with ₹208.80 a year earlier. Monthly data consumption also increased to 43.7 GB per customer from 37 GB.

These numbers point to a customer base that is using more data and generating more revenue per user. But rising consumption does not automatically translate into proportionate revenue growth. The company still needs to convert usage into higher-value plans, additional subscriptions and greater adoption of services beyond basic connectivity.

Monetising Digital Services And AI Bets

Jio’s digital-services narrative is built on the idea that its network, customer base and technology stack can support businesses beyond telecom. Its reach gives it a ready distribution channel: it can introduce digital products to millions of existing customers without having to acquire every user independently.

The company’s fixed broadband business illustrates how it is extending that infrastructure into adjacent markets. Jio’s fixed broadband customer base grew from 11.2 Mn in March 2024 to 28.6 Mn in June 2026, including 14 Mn JioAirFiber customers. The fixed wireless access service uses its 5G infrastructure to connect homes without requiring a physical fibre connection to every premises, potentially making expansion faster in areas where laying fibre is difficult. 

The opportunity is significant because broadband can deepen household engagement beyond mobile data. JioHome combines connectivity with entertainment and smart-home services, while JioTV+ aggregates television channels and streaming services. JioAICloud offers cloud storage with AI-supported features, and JioPC provides cloud-based computing. JioAICloud had approximately 66 Mn registered users as of June 30, 2026, according to the RHP. 

However, registered users are not the same as paying subscribers, and this is where the distinction between reach and monetisation becomes critical. A large user base can help a platform distribute new products, but the financial value depends on conversion rates, repeat usage, willingness to pay and the cost of delivering the service. 

The same scrutiny applies to Jio’s AI ambitions. The company says its proprietary AI engine, JioBrain, is embedded across network operations to support capacity allocation, fault prediction, resolution and real-time optimisation. It intends to extend these capabilities to other telecom operators and enterprise customers, alongside AI-powered customer services and automation tools. 

These ambitions could open up a different growth avenue. Rather than earning primarily from millions of individual mobile subscriptions, Jio could potentially sell technology, network-management capabilities and enterprise AI solutions to businesses. But this remains a proposition that is yet to prove.

What Does Jio Platforms Offer Beyond Scale? 

Jio enters the public markets with a sizable customer base, expanding revenue and strong EBITDA margins. But the IPO valuation puts the spotlight on how much growth investors are already paying for.

At the upper end of the ₹1,119 price band, Jio Platforms is valued at around ₹10.3 Lakh Cr. This gives the listing importance beyond the company itself: it will create a standalone market benchmark for a business that has so far been housed within Reliance Industries.

Brokerage comparisons with Bharti Airtel underline the debate. Nomura estimates Jio’s implied FY28 enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiple at around 10.5-10.9X, compared with 9.2X for Airtel’s India telecom business. 

The comparison also highlights the role of tariffs in future earnings. A price increase could lift ARPU across the sector, but the impact will depend on how customers respond, including whether they upgrade or downgrade plans, or leave the network. 

Jio’s wide customer base gives it reach, but its ability to translate higher prices into sustained revenue growth will depend on customer retention and the value it delivers. The one thing in Jio’s favour in this regard is that it has just Airtel as the competition at the top end. The two big players usually raise prices in unison which leaves little room for customer attrition. 

The IPO’s use of proceeds presents another important consideration. Jio Platforms plans to use up to ₹27,500 Cr of net proceeds to prepay, in full or in part, certain borrowings taken by RJIL, with the balance available for general corporate purposes subject to the offer-document conditions. This makes the issue partly a balance-sheet exercise. If it wasn’t clear already, this means investors should not treat the proceeds as funding that will automatically translate into new growth projects. 

The offering is also a fresh issue rather than an offer for sale, meaning the proceeds go to the company rather than existing shareholders selling down their holdings. RIL is expected to remain the controlling shareholder after the listing, with its stake declining from around 66.4% to approximately 64.5% following the issue. 

The company will also need to continue investing in infrastructure as data usage grows and technologies evolve. Strong EBITDA margins offer financial capacity, but, for investors, the billion-dollar question is whether Jio’s digital ambitions can live up to its lofty valuation.

Can Tonbo Imaging Justify Its Valuation? The defence tech startup’s ₹852.9 Cr IPO received strong early demand amid rising investor interest in India’s defence tech sector. But at a valuation of around ₹4,010 Cr, Tonbo must convert its order pipeline into sustained growth and stronger cash generation to justify investor expectations.

item.title: Starlink, Jio & OneWeb: Untangling The Satcom Queue
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: The irony was not lost on many. Around the same time as the internet in India’s national capital Delhi was…
item.content:encoded:
The irony was not lost on many. Around the same time as the internet in India’s national capital Delhi was shut down for several hours amid massive security and incessant protests, SpaceXAI chairman and founder Elon Musk waded into one of his quintessential Twitter feuds with the Indian government over Starlink and its satellite internet services.

This time, his target was not just the Indian government. Musk took on Reliance Jio — and then Mukesh Ambani too — accusing the conglomerate of strong-arming the government into creating a monopoly when it comes to satellite internet or satcom services. He even called Ambani the Prime Minister of India.

“Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license?” Musk posted, asking whether Ambani is the “real boss of India”.

Out came the responses from all quarters of India.

Reliance Industries rejected suggestions that it fears competition, saying it welcomes satellite broadband players, including Starlink, provided they follow Indian laws and policies. Reliance also pointed out that Jio’s satellite services are awaiting clearances.

The Ministry of Communications, meanwhile, has denied allegations of unequal treatment. It said the authorisation framework is fair and non-discriminatory, and that Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are at “broadly the same regulatory stage.”

And then, Starlink responded to Reliance saying, “We have worked closely with regulators, industry and operators in India for 5+ years, and built a network of dedicated systems, gateways, and other infrastructure all in-country to exclusively serve Indian traffic safely and securely – and all with the requisite government approvals.”

Everyone’s Waiting In The Queue

The immediate question is what Starlink means by having the “requisite government approvals”. Its statement does not explicitly say that its security assessment is complete or that spectrum has been assigned. Those are separate steps from obtaining a satellite communications licence and an IN-SPACe authorisation, and they stand between the operators and commercial launch.

The DoT has taken a similar line on the approval process. It said all three operators have received GMPCS licences and that security assessments remain underway. Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite (GMPCS) is a satellite-based communication system that provides voice, data, fax, and messaging services directly to portable terminals anywhere on ground.

The DoT added that spectrum assignment will follow once the relevant assessments are complete.

So a licence does not, by itself, authorise a company to start commercial services. Operators must meet the conditions attached to their services, clear the security process and complete spectrum-related requirements.

The dates of approvals have become part of the debate. Eutelsat OneWeb received its GMPCS licence in August 2021 and IN-SPACe authorisation in November 2023. Jio’s satellite communications arm received its GMPCS licence in March 2022. Starlink received its GMPCS licence in June 2025 and IN-SPACe authorisation in July 2025.

However, this timeline does not tell the full story. According to a Financial Express report citing DoT records, Jio Satellite Communications Limited (JSCL) completed its security and technical compliance demonstration on March 20, 2025, while Eutelsat OneWeb conducted its demonstration in January 2025. Starlink’s demonstration took place only in early 2026.

So if anything, OneWeb should be ahead of Starlink and Jio in the queue after the final assessments.

Bharti Enterprises chairman Sunil Bharti Mittal said OneWeb had applied for approval five years ago, its ground network had been ready for three years, and its satellites had been positioned over India for around five years. Mittal added OneWeb would be happy to receive approval “at least a few days before him [Musk].”

The different timelines do not, on their own, establish that one company has been favoured or that others are being held back. They also do not explain what conditions remain outstanding or unfulfilled in each case. Therefore, the relevant questions are which requirements each operator has met, what is still pending and whether the same standard and timelines apply to all three players.

This will help us get to the bottom of the questions that Musk has raised.

The Regulator Takes Its Time

Sohom Banerjee, a public policy and technology strategist and founder of Quantive Advisory LLP, said the delay raises questions about regulator predictability, but is not in itself proof of unequal treatment. A fair process, he argued, requires equivalent security standards, documented criteria, clarity on outstanding requirements and a defined next step for each applicant.

Banerjee also cautioned against treating proposed timelines for one regulatory stage as deadlines for the entire process. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s suggested 30-day window for spectrum assignment and objections relates to a stage after prior in-principle network clearance. It should not be interpreted as a deadline for completing security assessments.

The criteria for security assessment are not open for public discussion or consultation, but given that internet services are critical not just for civilian use but also defence infrastructure, experts presume that such assessments may not necessarily take the same time for each applicant.

The approval process involves four distinct steps: a GMPCS licence, IN-SPACe authorisation, security assessment and spectrum assignment. Conflating them and calling this a single approval is what complicates the narrative.

Starlink May Be Ready, But Is That All It Takes?

Starlink’s latest statement is a claim about its preparation and infrastructure, but this does not indicate anything about whether the Indian government has completed its diligence when it comes to the security assessment.

While Starlink says it has built dedicated systems and gateways in India to serve Indian traffic, and that these have the requisite government approvals, this is not a guarantee of spectrum allocation.

The distinction is also relevant to Reliance Jio. In its IPO papers, Jio Platforms identified satellite broadband as a potential competitor to JioFiber and JioAirfiber, particularly in areas where terrestrial networks are expensive or difficult to deploy.

It also flagged that administrative allocation of satellite spectrum could give satellite operators a different cost structure from terrestrial telecom players that acquire spectrum through auctions. 

It’s imperative to understand the structure. Jio Satellite Communications Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Jio Platforms, was incorporated in October 2021 to provide communications services, including satellite-based connectivity.

It reported revenue from operations of ₹34.3 Cr in FY26 up from ₹10.7 Cr in FY25, against no revenue in FY24. The company reported ₹10.5 Cr for the quarter ended June 30, 2026. These figures relate to the subsidiary and should not be read as revenue from a launched retail satellite broadband service.

The filings also identify uncertainties around the timing, approvals and competitiveness of Jio’s own satellite plans. The company therefore has a commercial stake in the rules governing satellite broadband, even as its services await clearance.

And indeed, that has to be made amply clear: no company has launched satellite internet services in India yet.

Banerjee said predictable regulation does not mean relaxing security checks. It means setting out the criteria, identifying the authority responsible for each decision and communicating what remains to be done.

Security checks are central to satellite broadband because the operator controls parts of a communications network that may be used in strategically sensitive areas. The assessment needs to establish how India can retain oversight of network operations, access to sensitive information and service continuity.

One could also argue that this is a cultural difference, that Musk is used to a different governance approach when it comes to such matters. A security clearance is part of the overall approvals in the US, for example, and not a separate process.

Tarun Wig, cofounder and CEO of Innefu Labs, said foreign-controlled satellite networks can create risks around data sovereignty, service continuity and external control over critical communications infrastructure, particularly during conflicts. Starlink’s role in Ukraine has brought those concerns into focus, he said, though the circumstances there do not automatically mean India would face the same risks.

Wig said India should have a security framework in place before these services launch. He pointed to data protection and localisation requirements where necessary, network security audits, encryption, lawful interception under Indian law, incident reporting and safeguards against unauthorised access and cyberattacks.

Banerjee spoke on the operational control aspects of the security assessment. He believes that relevant checks could examine who can activate terminals, change routing or coverage, access sensitive network information and suspend services. Domestic control over key network functions, auditable access, terminal identification, restrictions in sensitive areas and clear incident-reporting processes likely also form part of the assessment.

The commercial case for satellite broadband is clear in places where fibre and mobile networks are difficult or costly to extend. TRAI data for August 2026 recorded 48.63 Mn wired broadband connections and 19.34 Mn fixed wireless connections. Satellite services could help connect remote communities and businesses including mines, energy sites, schools and health centres. Their reach will depend on pricing, network capacity and the conditions attached to spectrum.

The government’s position is that all three operators remain subject to the same security process. But to settle questions about delay and unequal treatment, it will need to make the next steps clearer: which requirements remain pending for each operator, who must sign off and what needs to happen before spectrum is assigned.

Starlink says it’s ready to launch but is not being allowed to. Reliance says it doesn’t fear competition. OneWeb says it’s also waiting in the queue. Ultimately, no one has launched anything yet, so all of this seems more like a case of Musk’s impatience.

Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam
