item.content:encoded:
Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets.

The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership.

Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. 

“⁠Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership.

Building on the momentum, fifteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses.

Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty seven startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs.

However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. 

“IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42.

There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation.

Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub.

Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026

AceVector

Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands.

The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025.

Almost a year later in September 2026, AceVector filed its red herring prospectus with the SEBI, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS component of up to 4.16 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. 

Subsequently, AceVector’s public issue was oversubscribed 4.93X, receiving bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. 

The company eventually made a weak debut on the exchanges on October 5. Shares of AceVector listed at ₹28.30 on the BSE, a discount of 11.6% to its issue price of ₹32 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹28.32, an 11.5% discount to the IPO price.

On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹395 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, losses also shrank nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr versus ₹126.3 Cr in FY25.

Amagi 

Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. 

The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services.

The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares.

Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. 

The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price.

Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr.

Aye Finance

Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO.

In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. 

Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr.

The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. 

On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. 

ESDS Software Solution

Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida.

The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh.

Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. 

ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025.

As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. 

Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X. Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429.

On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. 

On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25.

Fractal 

Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. 

Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn.

In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. 

The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900.

On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. 

Kissht

Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property.

The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast.

 The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. 

As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X.

Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price.

On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. 

Klassroom

Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. 

It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country.

The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. 

It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X.

Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. 

On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25.

LEAP India

A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. 

Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON.

LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures.

The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility.

Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. 

In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. 

The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer.

Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE.

Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25.

Moneyview

Founded in 2016 by Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview started off as a personal finance platform before pivoting to digital lending. Today, it offers services such as UPI payments, gold SIPs, fixed deposits, digital gold, home loans, BNPL and insurance.

The company claims to manage over  ₹19,800 Cr in AUM and has raised more than $250 Mn in funding. It competes with players like listed fintech MobiKwik, IPO-aspirant Navi, and MoneyTap. It entered the unicorn club in 2024.

In March 2026, the fintech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO. It then received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in late-June 2026.

In September 2026, the fintech unicorn filed its RHP. outlining an IPO with a fresh issue of shares worth ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of up to 10.04 Cr equity shares. The startup’s public issue then closed with an oversubscription of 98.46X, led by QIBs and NIIs. 

The digital lender made a bumper debut on the exchanges on October 1, with its shares listing at ₹55.6 on the BSE, a premium of 64% over the issue price of ₹34. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹55, marking a premium of nearly 62% over the issue price. 

Moneyview’s operating revenue grew 43.3% to ₹3,351.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,339.1 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, net profit rose a marginal 1% to ₹242.7 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹240.3 Cr in FY25.

Purple Style Labs

Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury house of brands featuring fashion labels like Pernia’s Pop Up Studio & Shop, Wendell Rodricks, and Hemant Trevedi. It operates over 12 Pernia’s Pop-Up Studio experience centres across India.

Backed by Alchemy Capital Management, Bajaj Holdings and Investment, and Minerva Ventures, the startup has raised more than $78 Mn to date.

In September 2025, the D2C brand filed its DRHP with SEBI for its public issue and received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. 

It then filed its RHP with SEBI in August 2026 for a public issue, which consisted entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. 

Subsequently, Purple Style Labs’ public issue opened for subscription in late August 2026 and closed with an oversubscription of 1.29X, receiving bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. 

Shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on September 7. The stock listed at ₹535 on the NSE, 6.96% lower than the issue price of ₹575. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹539, representing a discount of 6.26%.

On the financial front, the startup’s consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 as against ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25.

RentoMojo 

Founded in 2014 by Geetansh Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo is an omnichannel rental platform to lease appliances, furniture, and furnishings. The startup operates an app, website and physical stores. It operates 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. 

Backed by Accel, Chiratae Ventures and Bain Capital, the startup has raised over $45 Mn in funding to date.

Hopping on the IPO bandwagon in March 2026, the rental platform filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO and received SEBI’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026.

In September 2026, the startup finally filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.7 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹384-₹404 per share for its IPO.

The public issue opened for bidding on September 9 and closed on September 11. The IPO was oversubscribed 72.88X, receiving bids for 158.68 Cr shares against the 2.18 Cr shares on offer.

Shares of RentoMojo made a strong stock market debut on September 17. The stock listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over its issue price of ₹404. On the BSE, RentoMojo opened at ₹480, up 18.81% from the issue price.

The IPO opened despite RentoMojo cofounder and former COO Nain earlier filing a petition before the NCLT’s Bengaluru bench to stall the IPO proceedings. 

Alleging oppression and mismanagement, the plea claimed that incomplete or inaccurate information was shared with him and sought to declare his 2023 sale of 2,223 shares void ab initio.

On the financial front, RentoMojo reported a profit after tax of ₹104.3 Cr in FY26, up 142% from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr during the year under review from ₹266 Cr in FY25. 

SEDEMAC

Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications.

The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. Backed by Xponentia Capital Partners, A91 Partners, and 360 ONE Asset, SEDMAC has raised over $107 Mn to date.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the deeptech company filed its DRHP with SEBI in November 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in February 2026. 

Its public issue comprised solely an OFS component of up to 80.43 Lakh shares. The IPO was oversubscribed 2.68X, with investors cumulatively bidding for 1.51 Cr shares against 56.32 Lakh shares on offer.

Shares of the company made a stellar debut on the exchanges on March 11, listing at a premium of 13.5% on the NSE. The stock opened at ₹1,535 as against the issue price of ₹1,352 per share. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹1,510, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price.

SEDEMAC reported a net profit of ₹71.4 Cr in the first nine months of FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹770.66 Cr during the period under review. 

Shadowfax

Founded in 2015 by Vaibhav Khandelwal and Abhishek Bansal, Shadowfax is a logistics company that offers hyperlocal and on-demand delivery solutions for businesses.

Competing with the likes of Delhivery, LoadShare and Pickrr, the logistics major is backed by names such as Flipkart, Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), IFC, Nokia Growth Partners, Qualcomm and Trifecta Capital.

Shadowfax pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 for an IPO, and received markets regulator’s nod in October 2025. It filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in November 2025. The company’s IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹1,000 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹907 Cr. 

The company’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.72X, receiving total bids for 24.23 Cr shares against 8.9 Cr on offer. 

Subsequently, shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on January 28. The stock listed at ₹112.60 apiece on the NSE, a discount of 9.19% to the issue price of ₹124. On the BSE, shares of the logistics unicorn debuted at ₹113, down 8.87% below the issue price. 

In H1 FY26, the logistics unicorn’s net profit more than doubled to ₹21 Cr from ₹9.8 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue surged 68.4% YoY to ₹1,805.6 Cr during the period.

Shiprocket

Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Vishesh Khurana, Akshay Gulati, and Gautam Kapoor, Shiprocket aggregates third-party logistics providers. It claims to partner 17 courier firms like Delhivery, FedEx, Aramex, Xpressbees, DTDC, and Shadowfax and serves over 24,000 pin codes across India.

The logistics unicorn has raised over $323 Mn to date from investors like Temasek, Bertelsmann, Tribe Capital, Lightrock, and Zomato.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the Zomato-backed unicorn in May 2025 confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI and received the regulator’s approval in October 2025. Shiprocket then filed its RHP with the markets regulator in August 2026.

The logistics major’s ₹1,617 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹885.5 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹732 Cr. 

Subsequently, in mid-August 2026, Shiprocket’s public issue opened to healthy market response and closed with an oversubscription of 99.38X, receiving bidding for 938.53 Cr shares against 9.44 Cr shares on offer. 

Shares of the company made a strong debut on the D-Street on August 19. The stock listed at ₹131 on the NSE, marking a premium of 35.05% to the issue price of ₹97. On the BSE, it debuted at ₹129.50, a premium of 33.51%.  

On the financial front, Shiprocket’s operating revenue rose 24% to ₹2,024 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,632 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, net loss widened over 6% to ₹79.2 Cr during the fiscal from ₹74.5 Cr in FY25.

Turtlemint

Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurtech platform that enables financial advisors to distribute car, bike, health, and term life insurance to their customer networks. It claims to serve over 3 Lakh advisors nationwide.

The startup has raised more than $197 Mn to date from investors such as Amansa Capital, Jungle Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Vitruvian Partners, and Nexus Venture Partners.

In September 2025, Turtlemint pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI, and secured market regulator’s approval three months later in December.

Subsequently, the insurtech unicorn filed its RHP in June 2026. The IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹660.7 Cr and an OFS of 1.46 Cr shares.

Its public issue opened on June 19 and closed on June 23, with an oversubscription of 1.2X.

Despite this, the startup made a muted debut on the bourses on June 29. 

Shares of the insurtech startup listed at ₹134.90 on the NSE, a discount of 11.25% to the issue price of ₹152. On the BSe, the stock listed at ₹136.2 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 10.4% to the issue price.

The insurtech company’s net loss rose 19% to ₹184.7 Cr in the first nine months (9M) of FY26 as against a net loss of ₹154.7 Cr in the year-ago period. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 80% to ₹741.1 Cr from ₹411.1 Cr in 9M FY25.

The startup designs and manufactures its products in India and sells them via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. Backed by names such as Steadview Capital, Jungle Ventures and A91 Partners, Atomberg has raised over $126 Mn in funding to date.

Founded in 2016 by Varun Dua and Ruchi Deepak, Acko is an insurtech platform that sells automobile, health, and travel insurance. It also offers embedded insurance solutions to ecommerce and travel tech companies.

Backed by marquee names like General Atlantic, Amazon and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPPIB), the startup has raised $458 Mn to date. It achieved the unicorn valuation during its $255 Mn Series D fundraise in 2021. 

In April, the startup roped in ICICI Securities, Morgan Stanley, and Kotak Securities as the bankers to helm its upcoming IPO, which will comprise both fresh issue and an OFS. The startup is said to be looking to raise $300 Mn to $400 Mn via its public issue at a likely valuation of $2 Bn to $2.5 Bn.

Acko is looking to file its DRHP via the confidential route in the second half of 2026 and is eyeing a listing in the first half of 2027.

Ahead of its potential D-Street debut, the startup laid off around 60 employees, or nearly 5% of its total workforce, to streamline its operations, citing AI-led automation.

On the financial front, Acko reported a net loss of ₹424.4 Cr in FY25, down 57% from ₹669.9 Cr the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 35% to ₹2,836.8 Cr from ₹2,106 Cr in FY24.

Battery Smart

Founded in 2019 by Pulkit Khurana and Siddharth Sikka, Battery Smart operates a battery-as-a-service platform that enables commercial electric two- and three-wheelers to swap discharged batteries for fully charged ones within minutes.

The startup claims to have built a network of more than 1,500 swapping stations across 75+ cities. It has so far deployed over 3 Lakh lithium-ion batteries and nearly 1 Lakh commercial EV drivers use its network. 

It has raised more than $200 Mn to date from marquee names like Tiger Global, Orios Venture Partners, FAAD Network, Blume Ventures and Trifecta Capital.

Battery Smart’s IPO plans first came to light in August 2026 after reports surfaced that the startup was looking to file its DRHP with SEBI by October 2026. There appears no clarity so far on its public issue size and the valuation it plans to seek.

On the financial front, the startup’s net loss widened nearly 93% to ₹27 Cr in FY25 as against ₹14 Cr in the year ago fiscal. However, revenue from operations zoomed 52% to ₹249 Cr during the fiscal under review compared to ₹164 Cr in FY24.

BRND.ME (Formerly Mensa Brands)

Founded in 2021 by ex-Myntra CEO Ananth Narayanan as Mensa Brands, BRND.ME is a house of brands that initially acquired 20 D2C brands to scale them. It became the fastest Indian startup to enter the unicorn club in 2021, attaining the coveted $1 Bn valuation within six months of its inception. 

It rebranded to its new identity last year and operates consumer brands such as Pebble, MyFitness, Dennis Lingo, among others. The unicorn has raised more than $300 Mn in funding till date from the likes of Accel, Alpha Wave Global, Norwest Venture Partners, Tiger Global, and Prosus.

The company is looking to list on the Indian bourses by 2027. Ahead of the IPO, the unicorn received approvals from National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in February 2026 to redomicile back to India from Singapore. 

On the financial front, BRND.ME saw a 5.8% decline in operating revenue to $168 Mn (about ₹1,394 Cr) in FY25 from $178.6 Mn (about ₹1,482 Cr) in the previous fiscal. Meanwhile, its loss widened 39% to $60.4 Mn (about ₹501 Cr) from $43.5 Mn (about ₹361 Cr) in FY24.  

Captain Fresh

Founded in 2019 by Utham Gowda, Captain Fresh runs a B2B seafood platform that exports fish. It also operates a marketplace that connects fisherfolk with buyers. It also provides end-to-end operations management tools for retail outlets and supermarket chains.

Backed by Tiger Global, Prosus, and British International Investment (BII), the startup has raised over $172 Mn to date.

Captain Fresh took its first official step toward listing in July 2025 by converting to a public entity and dropping the word “private” from its name. Subsequently in August 2025, Inc42 reported that the startup had confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI for a $400 Mn public issue, split between a $200 Mn fresh issue and a $150-200 Mn offer-for-sale.

However, in late December 2025, the startup withdrew its DRHP from SEBI due to delays in regulatory clearances for an acquisition in Europe. Captain Fresh plans to refile papers in early 2026 once approvals are secured.

Captain Fresh flipped to profitability in FY25, posting a consolidated net profit of ₹42.4 Cr as against a loss of ₹229 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Operating revenue skyrocketed 145% to ₹3,421 Cr from ₹1,395 Cr in FY24.

CarDekho

Founded in 2008 by siblings Amit Jain and Anurag Jain, CarDekho Group operates an online car listing platform, insurtech platform InsuranceDekho, lending platform Rupyy, and other brands. 

The startup has so far raised more than $750 Mn in funding to date and competes with the likes of CarTrade, Spinny and Cars24.

CarDekho has been planning to list on the bourses for some time now. At first, it was internally mulling plans for an IPO in 2021, but the idea failed to take off. Afterwards in 2024, the unicorn once again began talks with merchant bankers for a public issue to raise nearly $500 Mn at a valuation of $2 Bn to $2.5 Bn. This plan also failed to materialise. 

The auto marketplace is now back on the IPO bandwagon. It has already lined up Axis Bank, IIFL, Goldman Sachs and Nomura as bankers to helm its listing. It is now looking to file its DRHP by September 2026 to raise up to ₹3,500 Cr via an IPO, which will comprise both fresh issue (10% of the total size) and an OFS. 

The unicorn is said to be eyeing a valuation of ₹13,000-15,000 Cr for the listing, higher than ₹9,000 Cr at which it was pegged during its last fundraise in 2021.

On the financial front, CarDekho Group’s consolidated operating revenue rose 24% YoY to ₹2,795 Cr in FY25, while net loss narrowed marginally to ₹266 Cr from ₹276 Cr in FY24.

Cars24

Founded in 2015 by Vikram Chopra, Gajendra Jangid, Mehul Agrawal, Ruchit Agarwal and Chopra, Cars24 operates an online marketplace that allows users to buy and sell pre-owned cars. 

It has lately also forayed into new segments like auto-focussed content commerce market with Team BHP and vehicle information platform space with CarInfo. Having raised more than $1.3 Bn to date, the startup entered the unicorn club in 2020 after its $200 Mn Series E fundraise. 

The auto tech major’s IPO plans came to light in January 2026 after cofounder and CEO Chopra said that Cars24 would list on the bourses in the next six to twelve months (July 2026 to January 2027). 

However, in September 2026, Cars24 CFO Shivanshu Makkar reportedly said that the used-car marketplace would be able to complete its reverse flip from Singapore to India only by April 2027. It will then file its DRHP for an IPO.

If the plan materialises, Cars24 would become the second auto tech startup to go public, after rival CarTrade. 

On the financial front, Cars24’s operating revenue jumped 25% to ₹6,917.1 Cr in FY24 compared to ₹5,529.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Net losses also rose 7% to ₹498.4 Cr from ₹467.7 Cr in FY23.

Flipkart

Founded in 2007 by Binny Bansal and Sachin Bansal, Flipkart has grown from a small online bookstore into India’s largest ecommerce marketplace. Walmart acquired majority control in the ecommerce juggernaut in 2018 for $16 Bn. Since then, it has also expanded into fintech, travel tech and quick commerce.

Flipkart was last valued at $35 Bn after a $1 Bn fundraise in 2024. Arguably the biggest startup in the country by valuation, the decacorn received in-principle approval from a Singapore court in September 2025 to reverse flip back to India for its IPO. The plan was then cleared by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in December 2025.

Subsequently, the company redomiciled back to India in March 2026 after receiving the nod from the Indian government. A month later, reports surfaced that the ecommerce major was exploring raising a pre-IPO round of $2 Bn to $2.5 Bn from Indian and foreign investors. 

Taking a sharp U-Turn in May 2026, reports surfaced that Flipkart had deferred its IPO till at least 2028 to focus on profitability before its public listing. This came after parent Walmart directed the ecommerce company to focus on achieving EBITDA breakeven in FY27 itself.

The ecommerce major’s B2C arm, Flipkart Internet Private Ltd, reported an operating revenue of ₹20,493 Cr in FY25, up from ₹17,907 Cr in FY24. Meanwhile, losses also narrowed 37% to ₹1,494 Cr from ₹2,359 Cr, showing improved unit economics despite diversification.

Furlenco

Founded in 2012 by Ajith Mohan Karimpana, Furlenco operates a furniture and appliance rental platform across 28 cities like Bengaluru, Mumbai, Delhi NCR, Chennai, and Kolkata. With over 300 SKUs, the platform also sells new furniture.

Backed by Sheela Foam, Lightbox Ventures, Crescent Ventures, and White Oak, Furlenco has raised more than $290 Mn to date.

In September 2026, reports surfaced that the furniture and appliance rental startup had kicked off proceedings for a potential ₹1,000-1,200 Cr public issue. Furlenco is said to be close to appointing ICICI Securities as an advisor for its IPO, which will target a valuation of around ₹7,000 Cr. Furlenco is looking to launch the IPO in FY28.

The furniture rental startup turned profitable in FY25, with a net profit of ₹3.1 Cr as against a net loss of ₹130.2 Cr in FY24. Meanwhile, its revenue from operations spiked 64% to ₹228.7 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹139.6 Cr in FY24.

GoBoult

Founded in 2017 by Varun Gupta and Tarun Gupta, GoBoult (formerly Boult) is a smart wearables brand that sells a range of earbuds, smartwatches, neckbands and speakers. The company rebranded to a new name in August 2025 following a trademark infringement case filed by its rival boAt.

The bootstrapped startup competes with the likes of boAt, Noise and Pebble. GoBoult sells its products via its own website, online marketplaces, quick commerce platforms as well as 3,000 offline stores across India.

Kicking off its IPO plans, GoBoult cofounder Varun Gupta told Inc42 that the smart wearables brand is planning to file its DRHP with SEBI by November 2026. The company is eyeing a listing on the bourses by the summer of 2027. 

On the financial front, GoBoult reported an operating revenue of ₹762.9 Cr in FY25, up 9.4% from ₹697.2 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its profit stood at ₹24.2 Cr during the fiscal, a near 10X jump from ₹2.5 Cr reported in FY24. 

Imarticus Learning

Founded in 2012 by Nikhil Barshikar and Sonya Hooja, Imarticus Learning is an edtech platform that offers upskilling programs in finance, digital marketing, data analytics, GenAI, and others to individual learners and corporate employees.

The platform claims to have trained nearly 40,000 learners across B2C and B2B verticals. Backed by Global Ivy Ventures, Capian, and BLinC Invest, Imarticus has raised over $11.7 Mn to date.

In April 2025, cofounder and CEO Barshikar told Inc42 the company was looking to file its DRHP with SEBI for an ₹750 Cr IPO, which would comprise both fresh issue of shares and an OFS. However, there appears to be no clarity on this front so far.

While the company is yet to finalise its valuation for the IPO, bankers are said to have pitched a 25X to 30X revenue multiple for its valuation. Considering Barshikar’s claim of ₹205 Cr revenue in FY25, the edtech company could be staring at a valuation of ₹5,000 Cr to ₹6,000 Cr. 

Ahead of the IPO in August 2026, the edtech startup acquired Singapore-based BELLS Institute of Higher Learning for ₹800 Cr. 

On the financial front, Imarticus Learning’s revenue grew over 16% to ₹159 Cr in FY24 from ₹136.8 Cr in FY23, as per Tofler. Net losses, however, shot up nearly 10% to ₹24.6 Cr from ₹22.4 Cr in the year ago fiscal.

InMobi

Founded in 2007 by Naveen Tewari, Piyush Shah, Mohit Saxena and Abhay Singhal, InMobi is an adtech platform that offers a suite of product discovery and monetisation tools.

Based in Singapore, the SaaS company also maintains offices in Bengaluru, New York, Beijing,  and Dubai. With investments from Sherpalo Ventures, SoftBank, Kleiner Perkins, and others, InMobi has secured over $320 Mn in funding to date and was one of India’s earliest unicorns back in 2011.

Last heard, the startup was planning to file its DRHP with SEBI for a potential $1 Bn listing at a valuation of $8 Bn to $10 Bn. In July 2026, reports surfaced that the adtech unicorn had roped in four merchant bankers, namely JPMorgan Chase, Jefferies, Kotak Mahindra Capital and Axis Capital, to helm its upcoming $1 Bn (₹9,634 Cr) public issue.

However, this will not be InMobi’s first stab at an IPO. In 2021, it was reportedly planning for an IPO but shelved the plans due to adverse market conditions and funding winter.

Leverage Edu

Founded in 2017 by Akshay Chaturvedi, Leverage Edu is a study abroad platform that helps students apply to foreign universities. Its horizontal stack also spans offerings like fintech, accommodation, travel and career support. 

Besides its core app, it also offers test preparation courses for exams like IELTS and TOEFL. 

The startup claims to have so far catered to more than 1.75 Lakh customers. Leverage Edu has so far raised nearly $73 Mn from names such as Blume Ventures, DSG Consumer Partners, and Kaizenvest.

In April 2026, Inc42 reported that Leverage Edu had begun discussions with both domestic and international investment bankers for an IPO. The startup is looking to raise ₹2,000 Cr to ₹3,000 Cr via its public issue, which will comprise both fresh issue of shares and an OFS component. The platform is eyeing a valuation of over $900 Mn. 

In September 2026, Inc42 reported that the startup was looking to raise a ₹500 Cr as part of a pre-IPO round. Sources further added that the company is in the process of finalising merchant bankers for its public issue and will file its DRHP with SEBI by 2027-end.

On the financial front, Leverage Edu’s revenue from operations zoomed 91% to ₹173 Cr in FY25 from ₹90.6 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. In line with the top line, losses also rose nearly 56% to ₹106 Cr from ₹68 Cr in FY25. 

Mohalla Tech (ShareChat)

Founded in 2015 by IIT Kanpur alumni Ankush Sachdeva, Bhanu Pratap Singh and Farid Ahsan, Mohalla Tech operates social media platform ShareChat, short video platform Moj and subscription-based microdrama app QuickTV.

It has raised over $1.2 Bn in funding till date from names such as Lightspeed, Tiger Global, Temasek, Tencent, among others.

Kicking off its IPO plans, Mohalla Tech cofounder and CFO, Manohar Charan, told a publication that the startup is targeting a public listing to raise over $400 Mn in the next four to five quarters (FY28). 

On the financial front, ShareChat managed to narrow its adjusted EBITDA loss by 72% to ₹219 Cr in FY25 from ₹793 Cr a year ago. However, its operating revenue remained nearly flat at ₹723 Cr as against ₹718 Cr in FY24.

Navi                                                              

Founded in 2018 by Flipkart cofounder Bansal and Ankit Agarwal, Navi is a fintech startup that offers a range of financial services such as loans, digital payments, insurance, and mutual fund investments.

Reports in February 2025 first indicated that Navi was likely eyeing a public listing in the second half of FY26. However, the startup later deferred its IPO plans. 

Subsequently in August 2026, reports once again surfaced that Navi was planning to file its DRHP with SEBI by December 2026, eyeing a fresh issue-only IPO of about ₹3,000 Cr. The fintech unicorn is also said to have appointed JM Financial, Kotak Mahindra Capital, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan as advisers for the proposed offering. 

Ahead of the IPO, Dutch VC giant Prosus in August 2026 also invested $100 Mn in the fintech startup, marking the latter’s first institutional capital raise.

This isn’t Navi’s first attempt at going public. It first filed a DRHP with SEBI in 2022 for an  ₹3,350 Cr offering but scrapped the plan amid market turbulence.

On the financial front, Navi’s net loss widened 268.7% to ₹465.99 in FY26 from ₹126.4 Cr in the prior fiscal year. This came despite operating revenue increasing 16.8% to ₹2,981.7 Cr from ₹2,565 Cr in FY25.

OfBusiness

Founded in 2015 by Asish Mohapatra, Ruchi Kalra, Bhuvan Gupta, Chandranshu Sinha, Nitin Jain, Srinath Ramakkrushnan and Vasant Sridhar, OfBusiness runs a B2B ecommerce platform that sells construction materials and offers financing solutions to customers.

In November 2024, the startup roped in five investment banks, namely Axis Capital, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Citigroup, and Bank of America, to helm its IPO. Right after, CFO Bhavesh Keswani revealed plans for a $750 Mn to $1 Bn public issue. However, the plan did not materialise. 

Reviving its IPO plans two years later, reports once again surfaced in August 2026 that the B2B ecommerce unicorn was looking to file its DRHP with SEBI by November 2026. This time, it is eyeing a $800 Mn IPO, which could comprise a fresh issue of up to $260 Mn and a $540 Mn OFS. OfBusiness is said to be targeting a valuation in the range of $5-6 Bn.

On the financial front, the B2B ecommerce giant reported a 21% jump in its consolidated profit to ₹724 Cr in FY26 from ₹597 Cr in FY25. However, operating revenue remained largely flat YoY at ₹20,645 Cr. 

PayNearby

Founded in 2016 by Anand Kumar Bajaj and Yashwant Lodha Subhash Kumar, PayNearby utilises its network of local retail shop owners to facilitate digital financial services for its customers. Its offerings include cash withdrawals, remittances, bill payments, deposits, and insurance.

The fintech startup claims to have more than 12 Lakh retail partners under its belt and has raised nearly $4 Mn in funding to date.

Kicking off its IPO preparations, cofounder and CEO Bajaj shared in August 2025 that PayNearby is eyeing a FY27 listing. The company is also finalising a merchant banker as it looks to file its DRHP with the SEBI soon.

PayNearby’s standalone operating revenue slipped 4% to ₹355 Cr in FY24 from ₹368 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, profits fell 25% to ₹1.5 Cr from ₹2 Cr in FY23.

PayU India

Prosus-backed payments solutions provider PayU India’s IPO ambitions remain on hold. In June 2025, the Dutch giant announced it was deferring the listing to first strengthen its operations.

This was the third time that the company delayed its IPO plans. Early 2025 reports had suggested that PayU was gearing up to file its DRHP for a post-Q1 FY26 markets debut, but the plans failed to materialise.

Earlier in November 2023, Prosus’ then CIO Ervin Tu had projected readiness for a H2 2024 listing via a $500 Mn IPO. That plan also fizzled. 

The June 2025 postponement of the IPO followed a ₹1,013 Cr rights issue from parent Prosus in April 2025. Notably, a few months later in September, reports once again surfaced that the fintech major was looking to raise $250 Mn to $300 Mn in a pre-IPO round to broaden its investor base, test demand, and set a benchmark valuation for the listing.

As per parent Prosus’ annual report, PayU India’s revenue climbed 21% to $669 Mn in FY25 from $551 Mn in the year ago fiscal. The investor also claimed that PayU’s India payment arm broke even in H2 FY25  while adjusted earnings before interest and taxes (aEBIT) margin improved by 1 percentage point to -2% in the financial year under review.

Practo

Founded in 2008 by Shashank ND and Abhinav Lal, Practo helps patients book appointments with doctors for online consultations, order medicines, and book diagnostic tests. It also offers software solutions for doctors, clinics, and hospitals. The startup also operates 40 co-branded dermatology clinics across the country.

The health tech startup has raised nearly $230 Mn in funding to date from the likes of Tencent, Peak XV Partners (then Sequoia Capital), Z47 Partners (erstwhile Matrix Partners India), Sofina, among others. 

Practo was initially planning to list on the Indian bourses in 2026 but has now moved the IPO timeline to 2027. Ahead of the listing, in February 2026, reports surfaced that the startup was in advanced talks to raise up to $125 Mn in a pre-IPO round, in a mix of equity and debt, at a valuation of $700 Mn. 

The startup reported an operating EBITDA of ₹15 Cr on a revenue of ₹234 Cr in FY25. 

Rebel Foods

Founded in 2011 by Kallol Banerjee and Jaydeep Barman, Rebel Foods is a cloud kitchen unicorn that operates multiple quick service restaurant (QSR) brands such as Behrouz Biryani, Ovenstory Pizza, The Good Bowl, SLAY Coffee, Wendy’s, among others. 

The startup has so far amassed over $563 Mn in funding from the likes of Coatue Management, Lightbox, Peak XV Partners, and Temasek. The startup was last pegged at $1.4 Bn during its last $25 Mn fundraise from Qatar Investment Authority in April 2025. 

The company’s IPO plans first came to light in October 2024 after reports surfaced that Rebel Foods was looking to list on the bourses in the next 18 months (April 2026). However, the company is yet to even file its DRHP. 

However, in a major top-level rejig in July 2025, the company’s cofounder and India CEO Ankush Grover was appointed as global CEO, while incumbent Jaydeep Barman was elevated to the role of chairman and group CEO.

On the financial front, the unicorn’s net losses shrank 12% to ₹336.6 Cr in FY25 from ₹380.3 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenues grew 14% to ₹1,617.4 Cr from ₹1,420.2 Cr in FY24.

Servify

Founded in 2015 by Sreevathsa Prabhakar, Servify is a B2B device management platform that offers protection plans, buybacks, and exchanges. The startup earns a majority of its revenue from sale of services such as device protection plans and platform licences.

Besides India, it also operates in the US, Canada, China and the Middle East. The startup has raised nearly $130 Mn in funding to date from BEENext, Blume Ventures, DMI Sparkle Fund, Iron Pillars, and others.

Inc42 exclusively reported in January 2025 that the Mumbai-based startup had enlisted three investment bankers for a $400 Mn to $500 Mn IPO at a likely valuation of $1.5 Bn. The offering will likely lean heavily on OFS (55-60%), with the remaining 40-45% reserved for fresh issue of shares. 

Servify was previously looking to list on the exchanges by Q1 2026, but the plan looks far-fetched as the company is yet to even file its draft IPO papers with the markets regulator. 

Meanwhile, Servify saw hefty improvement on the financial front in FY24 as loss shrank 59% YoY to ₹93.81 Cr. This came largely on the back of operating revenue increasing 23% YoY to ₹754 Cr in the fiscal under review. 

Spinny

Founded in 2015 by Niraj Singh, Mohit Gupta, and Ganesh Pawar, Spinny operates a full-stack marketplace that enables users to buy and sell certified used cars. Unlike aggregators, the platform owns the inventory and refurbishes cars in-house.

Backed by marquee names such as Fidelity, Accel, Tiger Global, General Catalyst and WestBridge Capital, the startup has raised more than $784 Mn in funding to date. It was last valued at around $1.5 Bn during its $170 Mn fundraise, which was a mix of primary and secondary deals, in early-2026.

It competes with the likes of CARS24, CarDekho, and Droom in India’s growing used car market.

Kicking off its IPO proceedings, Spinny, in April 2026, roped in Kotak Mahindra Capital, Morgan Stanley, and Citigroup as bankers for its potential IPO. 

In September 2026, the startup pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI via the confidential route. The Gurugram-based startup is looking to raise ₹2,500 Cr to ₹3,000 Cr through a combination of fresh issue and an OFS component. It is targeting a potential listing in 2027.

On the financial front, Spinny’s net loss declined 28% to ₹423.8 Cr in FY25 from ₹590.3 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue rose 25% to ₹4,656.1 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹3,730 Cr in FY24.

Square Yards

Founded in 2014 by husband-wife duo Tanuj Shori and Kanika Gupta Shori, Square Yards runs a full-stack proptech platform for property search, property management tools, and home interior financing.

The startup has raised more than $200 Mn in funding from Reliance Group, ADM Capital, Bennett Coleman & Co Ltd (BCCL), Genkai Capital, and others.

In May 2026, Square Yards’ CFO Piyush Bothra told Inc42 that the company was looking to rope in bankers to explore a $250-300 Mn IPO in the next 12 months. 

If the IPO materialises, Square Yards will be among a handful of Indian startups where founders will continue to hold more than 50% stake. 

On the financial front, the proptech startup clocked an operating revenue of ₹2,086 Cr in FY26 on a gross profit of ₹476 Cr.

Udaan

Founded in 2016 by Vaibhav Gupta, Sujeet Kumar and Amod Malviya, Udaan operates a B2B-focused ecommerce platform. Operating across categories like FMCG, staples and fruits & vegetables, the platform also facilitates supply chain and logistics solutions for retailers. 

It also has a fintech platform called udaanCapital, which offers financial services to small businesses and helps them with their working capital requirements. 

Backed by marquee names such as Lightspeed, DST Global, Altimeter Capital and Tencent, Udaan has raised more than $2.17 Bn in funding to date.

In March 2026, Udaan’s cofounder and CEO Vaibhav Gupta told a publication that the company was eyeing a listing on the Indian bourses in the next nine to 18 months. Gupta added that the B2B ecommerce major plans to commence the process of redomiciling back to India from Singapore “soon”.

On the financial front, Udaan reported a 37% YoY decline in net loss to ₹1,055 Cr in FY25, while operating revenue also declined 20% YoY to ₹4,561 Cr during the fiscal under review.

Wonderchef

Founded in 2009 by celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor and Ravi Saxena, Wonderchef sells a range of kitchenware and home appliances such as coffee machine, mixer grinders, cast iron pans, among others. 

The startup sells its offerings via its own website, ecommerce platforms as well as its own exclusive business outlets (EBOs). Backed by the likes of Sixth Sense Ventures, Amicus Capital, Godrej Family Office, Malpani Group, among others, the brand has raised more than $30 Mn in funding to date. 

The D2C brand was mulling filing its DRHP with SEBI for an OFS-heavy IPO at a likely valuation of ₹1,800 Cr. This is double compared to Wonderchef’s last-known valuation of ₹900 Cr. 

The D2C brand’s net profit soared 300% to ₹6 Cr in FY25 as against a profit of ₹1.6 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Revenue from operations jumped 13.9% to ₹430 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹377.7 Cr in FY24.

Zypp Electric

Founded in 2017 by Akash Gupta and Tushar Mehta, Zypp offers EV-based mobility solutions for delivery workers. Besides the core EV leasing business, it also operates EV battery swapping, maintenance and servicing infrastructure.

It also runs an advertising business and has developed a fleet management software platform, called Fleekies.ai.

Backed by the likes of Japan’s ENEOS Group, 100Unicorns, Anthill Ventures and Venture Catalysts, the EV logistics startup has raised more than $75 Mn in funding to date.

In June 2026, cofounder and CEO Gupta told Inc42 that Zypp Electric has roped in Axis Capital, SBI Capital Markets and DAM Capital to manage its upcoming public offering. He said the startup is looking to raise up to $200 Mn (about ₹1,890 Cr) via its IPO within the next 18 to 24 months. 

Ahead of the listing, Zypp Electric is looking to raise a pre-IPO round in the range of $40-50 Mn from private equity firms and impact-focused funds. 

On the financial front, Zypp Electric’s revenue from operations zoomed 49% to ₹438 Cr in FY25 from ₹293 Cr in the previous year. Meanwhile, net loss widened 20.1% to ₹107.5 Cr from ₹89.5 Cr in FY24.

item.title: Burma Burma Parent’s FY26 Loss Surges 31X YoY To ₹15 Cr
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Restaurant chain Burma Burma’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Limited, saw its net loss skyrocket nearly 31X to ₹15.4 Cr in…
item.content:encoded:
Restaurant chain Burma Burma’s parent entity, Hunger Pangs Limited, saw its net loss skyrocket nearly 31X to ₹15.4 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26) compared to ₹50 Lakh in the previous fiscal year.

According to its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP), the restaurant chain’s revenue from operations also zoomed 46.6% to ₹155.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹106.1 Cr in FY25. 

Including other income of ₹1.5 Cr, Burma Burma’s total income stood at ₹157 Cr in FY26. 

On the operational front, the restaurant chain’s EBITDA also climbed 20.2% to ₹25.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹21.4 Cr in the year ago fiscal. 

Besides its FY26 financials, the DRHP also shed light on the company’s Q1 FY27 numbers. Burma Burma’s parent reported a net profit of ₹1.1 Cr in the quarter under review against an operating revenue of ₹53.7 Cr. 

Given total expenses of ₹55.2 Cr during the quarter, what helped the company mint a profit in Q1 FY27 was ₹1.98 Cr in deferred tax credits. Burma Burma also reported an EBITDA profit of ₹11.4 Cr in the quarter ended June 2026, while the EBITDA margin stood at 21.3%. 

Founded in 2013 by Ankit Gupta and Chirag Chhajer, Hunger Pangs operates premium casual restaurant chain Burma Burma, which serves vegetarian Burmese cuisine. It competes with the likes of brands such as Mainland China, Mamagoto, Yum Yum Cha, and Berco’s.

At the end of July 2026, it operated 22 restaurants across nine cities, including Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kolkata, and Delhi NCR. 

After raising $4 Mn at a valuation of over $50 Mn earlier this year, the hospitality chain has now filed its DRHP with markets regulator SEBI. Its proposed IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹150 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of up to 2.8 Cr shares.

Of the fresh IPO proceeds, Burma Burma plans to use ₹117.3 Cr to open 27 new company-owned outlets by FY29. The remaining capital will be used for general corporate purposes. 

Notably, Hunger Pangs disclosed in its DRHP that it plans to launch a new brand. “We have conceptualised a premium casual dining chain of Japanese restaurants and noodle shops, with influences of Buddhist traditions,” read the document.

Where Did Burma Burma Spend In FY26?

In line with its revenue growth, Burma Burma’s spending also saw a major uptick. The company’s total expenses zoomed 61.8% YoY to ₹175.8 Cr in FY26. Let’s dive deeper into the company’s expenditure. 

Employee Benefits Expenses: Representing the company’s largest cost head, Burma Burma’s personnel costs surged 53.3% YoY to ₹50.7 Cr in FY26 from ₹33.1 Cr in the previous fiscal year.

Cost Of Materials Consumed: Burma Burma spent ₹30.4 Cr on raw materials and kitchen supplies in the fiscal under review, 51% higher than ₹20.1 Cr in FY25. 

Finance Cost: The restaurant chain’s interest and borrowing-related expenses grew 70% YoY to ₹6.6 Cr in the year under review. 

Other Expenses: Spending under this line item also grew 54.6% YoY to ₹48.8 Cr in the fiscal year ended March 2026.

item.title: Decoding Urban Company’s ₹2,500 Cr Fundraise Proposal
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Listed home services major Urban Company’s board approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr yesterday, seeking to shore…
item.content:encoded:
Listed home services major Urban Company’s board approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr yesterday, seeking to shore up its war chest at a critical juncture.

On one hand, Urban Company’s instant home services business, InstaHelp, is facing stiff competition. Fighting rivals Snabbit and Pronto for a slice of the market has turned out to be an expensive affair, with spending on InstaHelp contributing to Urban Company’s widening losses.

At the same time, the company is looking to expand its product lineup under the Native brand by entering the residential air conditioner market. Meanwhile, its bread and butter consumer services continue to generate stable results.

Urban Company’s financials reflect these pressures. The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr in Q2 FY27, driven by a ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding InstaHelp, it reported an adjusted EBITDA profit of ₹30 Cr.

During the quarter, consolidated revenue from operations grew 41.4% YoY to ₹537.3 Cr, while total expenses increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr. Consequently, the company’s consolidated net loss more than tripled to ₹182.5 Cr from ₹59.3 Cr in the year-ago period.

However, the management maintains that Urban Company can meet its profitability targets without the proposed fundraise Yet, the management has rejected the suggestion that the fundraise is necessary to offset InstaHelp’s impact on its financials.

How Badly Does Urban Company Need The Cash?

Urban Company has positioned the proposed ₹2,500 Cr fundraise as a means to bolster its balance sheet and provide greater flexibility to invest across its businesses.

“Our ambition is to go beyond being just a home services company and eventually become the trusted home platform for Indian consumers – almost the operating system for the Indian home. So given that ambition, we want the strategic flexibility over the next few years to invest in all our areas of business,” CEO Abhiraj Singh Bhal told analysts during the company’s Q2 FY27 earnings call.

The company also plans to deploy the capital towards growth opportunities, including acquisitions. While no acquisition deals have been finalised till now, the management is evaluating opportunities that could help Urban Company consolidate its position in an existing market or enter a new category.

Bhal added that the company would take an opportunistic approach to international markets and Native. However, an acquisition in InstaHelp would be “highly unlikely”.

“If at all we do an M&A, it would be to add on categories that we don’t operate in today where we feel that the decision of build versus buy may be tilting in favour of buy,” he noted.

Urban Company has guided for adjusted EBITDA breakeven by Q3 FY28 and ₹1,000 Cr in adjusted EBITDA profit by FY31. The management maintained that its current financial position, even without raising additional capital, is sufficient to meet these targets.

However, Bhal acknowledged that the company’s existing balance sheet limits its financial flexibility, given InstaHelp’s losses.

While the management maintains that the company can meet its profitability targets without additional capital, the proposed fundraise would provide it with greater room to invest in growth and respond to changing market conditions.

In particular, Urban Company is facing intense competition in the emerging quick home services segment. For instance, after Urban Company disclosed that InstaHelp completed 6.2 Mn orders in Q2, Snabbit’s founder Aayush Agarwal claimed that the startup had served 6.45 Mn orders during the period.

Diving Into A New Market

While it faces intense competition in the quick home services market, Urban Company is simultaneously looking to expand into a new category. 

Alongside approving the fundraise proposal, its board proposed exploring residential air conditioners as a new business under its consumer appliances brand Native, whose portfolio currently comprises water purifiers and smart locks.

“We’ve now operated in the segment of air conditioning servicing and repair for close to 11-12 years, ever since the inception of the company. And there’s a lot of data and knowledge that we have gathered on what are the consumer pain points and what are some of the unmet needs of the consumers. Based on those data points and our own understanding of the market and the unmet needs, we have been quietly working on creating an innovative cutting-edge product,” Bhal told analysts on the call.

The company is yet to disclose further details, including a commercial launch timeline. Notably, Inc42 reported last year about Urban Company’s potential foray into AC business.

Bhal said the first one to two years in the new market would focus on learning and gathering customer feedback. He also noted that Urban Company’s app would be the sole distribution channel for its ACs.

The CEO emphasised a “calibrated and measured” approach to capital allocation, adding that Native has a clear path to profitability that should not be affected by the new venture.

For context, Native’s net transaction value (NTV) grew 35.4% YoY in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue rose 40% to ₹105 Cr. The segment remained loss-making on an adjusted EBITDA basis, reporting a loss of ₹9 Cr. However, loss as a percentage of NTV declined to 6.8% from 9% a year ago.

Urban Company’s platform sees 10X as many AC servicing, repair, and installation orders as water purifier orders, giving it a larger existing customer base for AC-related services. This provides a potential channel to market Native’s ACs, although service demand does not necessarily translate into appliance sales. 

With InstaHelp facing stiff competition and Native preparing to enter a new product category, Urban Company is pursuing multiple growth opportunities even as its losses widen. The proposed fundraise would provide additional capital to support these plans, although the management maintains that the company can achieve its stated profitability targets without it.

item.title: Nazara, Groww Gain Among New-Age Tech Stocks This Week, AceVector Falls 18%
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Fewer than half of the 67 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage advanced this week despite a broader market recovery.…
item.content:encoded:
Fewer than half of the 67 new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s coverage advanced this week despite a broader market recovery. While 31 stocks gained between 0.03% and 17.63%, 36 declined, with losses reaching 18.43%.

Snapdeal parent AceVector was the biggest loser, falling 18.43% to ₹24.97, about 12% below its listing price.

Market intelligence platform Tracxn followed, declining 8.26% to ₹31.78. IndiQube and Veefin lost more than 7% each.

ixigo, EaseMyTrip, Swiggy, and Fractal touched fresh 52-week lows, while Nazara, Zelio, and E2E Networks hit fresh 52-week highs this week.

NSE SME-listed Yudiz led gains, surging 17.63% to ₹24.35, although it remained over 85% below its listing price. Nazara, ideaForge, DevX, and FirstCry were among the other gainers.

The combined market capitalisation of the 67 companies increased by $5.84 Bn to $160.55 Bn from $154.71 Bn at the end of the previous week.

Now, let’s take a look at the key developments at the new-age tech companies this week.

E2E Networks Swings To Profit

E2E Networks posted a consolidated net profit of ₹72.7 Cr in Q2 FY27 against a ₹13.5 Cr loss a year earlier. Operating revenue jumped 411% to ₹223.8 Cr from ₹43.8 Cr.

Separately, it paid fines of ₹10,000 each, plus GST, to NSE and BSE for failing to provide prior intimation of its August 31 board meeting. The cloud infrastructure company said it would strengthen compliance monitoring to prevent recurrence.

NCLT Dismisses Globalbees Insolvency Plea

The NCLT dismissed an insolvency application against FirstCry subsidiary Globalbees filed by Ashutosh Garg, Paritosh Garg, and Manju Agarwal over an alleged ₹64.92 Cr claim, plus 18% annual interest.

Separately, Globalbees extended the deadline for its ₹5.69 Cr sale of its entire 51.54% stake in textile brand Mush to November 30. The buyers are existing shareholder Nihar Gosalia and Vaishvik Brahmbhatt.


Fairfax Proposes Go Digit Stake Transfer

Fairfax proposed transferring its interests in Go Digit General Insurance and Go Digit Life Insurance to IDBI Bank. Separately, Fairfax India Holdings also proposed transferring its entire IIFL Capital Services stake to the lender.

The proposals follow the selection of a wholly owned Fairfax Financial subsidiary to acquire a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank for approximately ₹52,878 Cr. The transfers would expand IDBI’s insurance and investment services presence, subject to requisite approvals. 

Lenskart Faces Customs Demand

Lenskart received an order during the week demanding ₹6.59 Cr in differential customs duty and ₹6.58 Cr in penalty, totalling ₹13.17 Cr, plus unquantified interest.

The authority reclassified certain imported optical eyeframes with clip-ons. The company said it considers the order contestable and plans to appeal.

First Games’ GST Demand Reduced

Paytm joint venture First Games Technology received a ₹703.66 Cr GST demand for April 2018 to March 2023, down from ₹5,712 Cr proposed in an April 2025 show-cause notice.

An equivalent penalty and applicable interest are additional. First Games is evaluating its statutory options.

BlackBuck Restructures Loads Business

BlackBuck approved transferring its loads business to wholly owned subsidiary BlackBuck Transport Services through a slump sale to improve operational efficiency.

The business generated ₹88.74 Cr in FY26 revenue, equivalent to 12.6% of BlackBuck’s standalone total income, and had net worth of ₹98.8 Lakh.

Aequs’ Amalgamation Proposal Rejected

The Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ regional director of South Western Region rejected Aequs’ amalgamation with wholly owned subsidiaries AeroStructures Manufacturing India, Aequs Engineered Plastics, and Aequs Force Consumer Products.

The order cited non-compliance with Section 233 of the Companies Act: shareholder approval representing 88.9% of total share value against the required 90%, uncertain delivery of postal ballot notices, pending labour cases, and missing BSE and NSE no-objection certificates.

Aequs is considering refiling or seeking approval under Section 232.

With that, here’s a look at the performance of the broader market this week. 

IT Leads Market Recovery

The Sensex gained 3.11% to 74,729.27 this week, while the Nifty 50 rose 2.78% to 23,146.15. IT led sectoral gains at 11.72%, although participation beyond large-cap stocks remained muted.

Geojit Investments’ research head Vinod Nair attributed the recovery to improving rupee sentiment, softer crude prices, easing bond yields, and strong quarterly business updates. The IMF’s higher growth forecasts for India for FY27 and FY28 also supported sentiment.

Investors tracked RBI’s measures to manage public-sector oil marketing companies’ dollar demand and tighten rupee-linked forex derivatives rules. Effective October 16, banks’ minimum daily CRR maintenance rose to 99% of the prescribed requirement from 90%.

Inflationary pressures, elevated crude oil prices, and continued foreign investor outflows remained concerns for the market. FIIs remained net sellers for the ninth consecutive week, although their net selling moderated to ₹8,991 Cr from ₹30,294 Cr in the previous week. However, they turned net buyers yesterday, with net purchases of ₹1,166 Cr.

DIIs remained net buyers for the ninth straight week, investing ₹7,813 Cr. Month-to-date purchases of ₹48,168 Cr nearly offset FII selling of ₹48,769 Cr, according to Bajaj Broking.

Investors will track September infrastructure output, October flash PMI readings, and the minutes of RBI’s monetary policy committee meeting. Earnings of major lenders will also be in focus, alongside results from Infosys, Swiggy, Eternal, Dr Reddy’s Laboratories, and Tata Motors. 

Nair said sustaining the recovery would require earnings growth beyond IT, with financials, consumption, and industrials’ revenue and margins under scrutiny.

Now, let’s take a deeper look at the performance of Nazara Technologies and Groww this week:

Nazara Gains Amid Leadership Changes

Nazara gained 10.02% to ₹416.80 amid a reshuffle that saw founder Nitish Mittersain move from MD to a non-executive role.

The company’s board approved CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti’s five-year appointment as whole-time director, designated executive director, subject to shareholder approval. Arun Agrawal, former global CFO of Ness Digital Engineering, will succeed outgoing CFO Rakesh Shah. Whole-time director Rohit Sharma will step down from January 1, 2027.

The changes follow the $303 Mn acquisition of Spanish gaming companies Bluetile Games and BestPlay Systems and a ₹733.5 Cr preferential fundraise to finance it.

On the financial front, Nazara posted a ₹82.5 Cr loss in Q1 FY27, with operating revenue falling 14% YoY to ₹428.8 Cr. Bluetile’s EBITDA remained flat despite 54% revenue growth amid higher user acquisition costs.

Groww Gains Despite Flat Sequential Revenue

Groww gained 4.34% to close the week ₹200.70 after its Q2 FY27 net profit rose 54% YoY to ₹724.7 Cr and operating revenue increased 47.4% YoY to ₹1,501.5 Cr.

Sequentially, revenue was almost unchanged and profit fell 1.4% from ₹735 Cr. EBITDA slipped to ₹969 Cr from ₹971 Cr in the preceding June quarter.

Growth in margin trading and commodity derivatives offset a 14.3% QoQ decline in equity derivatives revenue. The company attributed the decline in equity derivatives revenue to adjustments following the closing auction system’s (CAS) introduction.

Expenses rose 28.5% YoY to ₹555.9 Cr, reflecting higher technology costs, AI-linked and other compute cost inflation, and ₹13 Cr in client reimbursements following a third-party market infrastructure institution’s operational issue.

Groww AMC’s assets under management rose 145% YoY to ₹7,179 Cr, although it posted a ₹8.3 Cr quarterly loss.

Separately, brokerage Jefferies reiterated its ‘Buy’ rating on Groww following SEBI’s changes to the CAS framework.

The revised rules include a shorter cash-market auction window and changes to the settlement-price calculation for index derivatives on expiry days. The updated framework is scheduled to be effective December 7, 2026.

Jefferies expects lower expiry-day volatility and regulatory uncertainty to benefit brokers more than exchanges, whose premium turnover has already recovered to pre-CAS levels.

The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as against 13 in FY25. At the same time, a growing number of startups turned profitable or moved closer to profitability after years of cost rationalisation to adjust to the new funding realities. 

Despite a tough Q4 for many startups due to geopolitical uncertainties, Indian startups are expected to improve their top and bottom line numbers in FY26.

Of the 102 startups in the tracker, 65, or about 63.7%, reported profits in FY26. However, the profitability picture remained uneven. Together, these 65 startups generated a net profit of ₹14,511.8 Cr, while the remaining 37 posted a cumulative loss of ₹30,950.8 Cr, underscoring that sustainable profitability remains a work in progress for a section of the ecosystem.

Even so, the scale of India’s startup ecosystem continued to expand. The 102 companies generated ₹4.75 Lakh Cr in operating revenue in FY26, a sharp 34.62% increase from ₹3.53 Lakh Cr in FY25.

item.title: Cleartrip’s FY26 Loss Widens 28% YoY To ₹805 Cr, Revenue Up 21%
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Flipkart-owned travel platform Cleartrip’s net loss widened 28.1% YoY to ₹805 Cr in FY26 from ₹628.4 Cr in FY25, as…
item.content:encoded:
Flipkart-owned travel platform Cleartrip’s net loss widened 28.1% YoY to ₹805 Cr in FY26 from ₹628.4 Cr in FY25, as its expenses continued to outpace revenue growth.

The online travel aggregator’s operating revenue grew 20.8% to ₹198.3 Cr during the year from ₹164.1 Cr in the previous fiscal. Including other income, Cleartrip reported total income of around ₹241.3 Cr, compared with ₹366.7 Cr in FY25. Other income declined 34.2% YoY to ₹43 Cr.

Meanwhile, spending on cashbacks and discounts rose 47.5% to ₹897.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹608.2 Cr a year earlier, outpacing top line growth.

Cleartrip generated ₹702.2 Cr from service charges and ₹378.4 Cr from commissions and incentives before accounting for cashbacks and discounts, taking the combined figure to around ₹1,095.7 Cr. These figures should be distinguished from the operating revenue reported in its financial statements.

Founded in 2006 by Hrush Bhatt, Matthew Spacie and Stuart Crighton, Cleartrip enables users to book flights, hotels, trains, buses and local activities through its website and app. Ecommerce major Flipkart acquired the company in 2021.

Cleartrip’s accumulated losses rose to ₹3,828 Cr as of March 31, 2026, from ₹3,023 Cr a year earlier. Its negative net worth also widened to ₹3,066 Cr from ₹2,262 Cr in FY25.

In its financial statements, the company said its ability to continue as a going concern depended on the success of its operations and its ability to secure funding. However, it added that its holding company, Flipkart Internet Private Limited, had provided a commitment and letter of financial support.

During FY26, Cleartrip borrowed ₹3,964 Cr from Flipkart Internet and repaid ₹3,653 Cr. Interest on these loans stood at ₹130.4 Cr for the year.

The widening loss comes as Cleartrip seeks to reduce its reliance on discounts and diversify beyond flight bookings. In July 2026, the company said it was targeting operational break-even by the end of FY27. Its plans include growing its hotels, trains and buses businesses and increasing revenue from ancillary services.

The company has also seen leadership changes in recent years. Anuj Rathi, who joined as CBO, stepped down in June 2025, less than a year after his appointment, to launch his venture, profound.me. 

He was succeeded by former Flipkart executive Manjari Singhal, who previously led the ecommerce company’s beauty, FMCG and general merchandise businesses as vice-president and business head.

Before Rathi’s departure, long-standing CEO Ayyappan Rajagopal resigned from Cleartrip in August 2024 to launch quick-commerce startup FirstClub.

Where Did Cleartrip Spend? 

Cleartrip’s total expenses increased 21.9% YoY to ₹1,045.9 Cr in FY26 from ₹858.2 Cr in FY25. Against operating revenue of ₹198.3 Cr, this translated into expenditure of ₹5.27 for every rupee earned from operations.

Advertisement & Sales Promotion: Cleartrip’s spending on advertising and sales promotion rose 30.9% YoY to ₹133.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹102.2 Cr a year earlier.

Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs increased 7.8% to ₹258.1 Cr from ₹239.4 Cr in FY25.

Payment Gateway Charges: Payment processing expenses rose 40% YoY to ₹110.1 Cr from ₹78.7 Cr.

Commission & Brokerage: Expenses under this head increased 33.2% YoY to ₹171.5 Cr from ₹128.8 Cr in FY25.

item.title: Flipkart’s Logistics Arm Ekart Cuts FY26 Loss By 98% To ₹26 Cr
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Instakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in the fiscal year ending March 2026 (FY26). Its…
item.content:encoded:
Instakart Services, the Flipkart-owned logistics company behind Ekart, nearly broke even in the fiscal year ending March 2026 (FY26). Its loss narrowed 98.3% to ₹26 Cr in the fiscal under review, compared to ₹1,508 Cr in FY25.

The brand’s revenue from contracts with customers fell 4.2% to ₹13,194 Cr in FY26, from ₹13,779 Cr in the previous fiscal year. In this, Flipkart itself contributed ₹9,112 Cr, or about 69% of the total operating revenue.

Operationally, logistics, transportation and shipping contributed the most share, approximately 50% to ₹6,419 Cr in the reported year. Revenue from this vertical plunged 39.5% YoY.

Ekart also generates revenue from collection services and warehousing services. Collection services income fell 68% to ₹510 Cr, while warehousing services income rose 44% to ₹2,212 Cr.

Including finance and other income of ₹418 Cr, Instakart’s total income fell 3.9% to ₹13,612 Cr in the year under review.

Founded in 2009 by Sachin Bansal and Binny Bansal as an in-house logistics entity within Flipkart, Ekart was spun off as a separate entity in 2016 to support the fulfillment services not only for Flipkart and Myntra but also for D2C brands, online sellers and retailers.

As of last year, the company claimed to be operating more than 7,000 trucks running daily across the length and breadth of the country, 70 fulfilment centres, 80 sortation facilities and 3500 delivery hubs to ensure timely delivery across 14,000 pin codes.

Earlier in July, Ekart opened its pan-India logistics network to MSMEs, D2C brands, FMCG companies, and enterprises, allowing external businesses to access the logistics infrastructure used by Flipkart.

The logistics arm has already operationalised more than 300 franchise outlets across Surat, Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru, and had plans to expand the network to over 1,000 outlets by the end of 2026.

Magnifying Ekart’s Spending

Ekart’s total expenses for the fiscal dipped by 13% YoY to ₹13,638 Cr in the year under review, while its costs stood at ₹15,673 Cr in FY25. Here is a closer look at where Ekart spent the highest:

  • Freight, Handling and Servicing Expenses: The spending under this head fell by 17.1% to ₹9,191 Cr in FY25 from ₹11,093 Cr in the previous financial year. Of the overall expenditure, freight costs comprised 67.4%.
  • Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, which include salaries, provident fund, gratuity, among others, shrunk by 24.9% to ₹958 Cr from ₹1,275 Cr in FY25. Further, it accounted for 7% of the overall expenses in FY26.
  • Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: These costs increased by 5% to ₹1,456 Cr from ₹1,387 Cr in FY25.
